TIIE STRIKE ON THE LONDON AND.
, NORTH.WESTERN RAILWAY.
TIIE porters' strike at.the goods station of
tho_London and North-Western Railway is a
much more serious affair than it appeared to
be at the first glance. An ordinary strike of
employed against employers is chiefly interest-
ing to the general public by the suffering and
loss it cause* to the parties immediately.con-
corned. A strike or lock-out on the railway,
however, is a sore inconvenience and heavy
loss to the publio, and its causes, progress, and
consequences are, therefore, of considerable
public) importance..
The -present quarrel is but a beginning.
• How it may spread or what it may end in
.nobody knows, and) were it settled to-morrow
nobody could tell how soon similar battles
mighthave to be fought over again; an cl, there.
fore, no time should be lost in laying down,
if such a thing be possible, fixed rules of
settlement that may be applied to all such
eases, or rather in setting up
.some authority
recognised by both sides, which shall have full
.power to deal with all such misunderstandings
when they arise.
We thinki it may b.') said, on tin 'part of
. working men, that they always engage very
reluctantly in contentions with their em-
ployers. But there are occasions when they
canna be avoided. Complications sometimes
arise not through wages, hours, or conditions
.of work, only, but in consequence of
personal treatment which involves self-
respect and .personal independence; and in
these latter eases employers' frequently offend
very
,grievously; and 'sometimes, through
• habit, almost unconsciously to themselves.
.They admit that working men haVe a right to
fix their own price for their labour, where
they have the power to enforce their dentands,
nor do they deny the right of the men to insist
on, so far as they can, the time they will work;
and other conditions) connected with their
employment. But they do not see with
sufficient vletume§s, nor, practically acknoiv-
-ledge, what is due to working men in civil
treatment, and in a frank and kindly eon-
sideration of such_ grievances as annoy men
in following their ordinary everyday emu
-
potions. _ _

This quarrel between the Directors and a
portion of the men in their employment is an
instance of this. The men felt that there were
several things connected with their employ-
ment which required adjustment, and they
agreed to meet together that they might put

these into some sort of shape, with the view
of bringing them under the notice of the
Directors, or whoever else had authority to put
them right. This 'as a legitimate and proper
step enough, and one which never ought to
have been interfered. with. But, unfortunately
the dread of union amongst the mon filled
those in authority with anger, and the men
who presided at this meeting was forthwith
discharged. Nothing could have been more
injudicious than this, as it struck directly
and in the most offensive, insulting, and
dangerous way possible at the men's right to
unite together for a oommon purpose—a right
now not denied to any class of men in England,
provided their objects are bounded by legal
limits.

This discharge of a fellow workman pro-
duced its fitting and natural result. The men
determined to combine for mutual protection
from the aggression and other offences of Mr.
GRENNISII, who in this ease, it seems, repre-
sented the Directors and exercised their power.
Tliis gentleman was not to be deterred, and
another of. the men who had made himself
slightly prominent was discharged, and orders
of discharge were procured for others. Here
then was an absolute declaration of war; a
challenge to the men before which they must
have bumbled themselves, or by accepting it,
stand forward together as one man and refuse
a dictation so over-bearing and unjust. Who
can wonder that as English working men,
living at the present hour when the rights of
labour are being successfully asserted on all
hands, that they chose the latter alternative,
or who can doubt that in doing s) they did
what was to be fairly expected from mon of
courage and honour ?. Naturally they asked
for the removal of the man who stood armed
in their presence to punish them for exercising
an undoubted right—au unquestioned and un-
questionable privilege. They made it known
that they would not remain in the employment
of the Company, if that man was retained in
authority over them. The Company to use the
ordinary phraseology:" refused to be dictated
to," and so the men left. During this time,
however, it is right to state that the men offered
to meet their employers with tt view to peaceable
arrangement. They were, however, officially
Informed by Mr. CA.wxwELL that the matter
did not admit of discussion. Reconsideration
after this was asked for by the men, pending
their notice to leave, but no answer was
returned ; therefore, on the Friday the men
left.

Of course, these who approve of the "high
hand." will insist that the Directors did right;
that they ought not, and cannot be dictated to
as to who they shall or shall not employ.
This may be conceded, but the men, on the
other band, ought not to be dictated to as to
whom they will or will not work under, or
work with. The tune was when the worker
was treated with little more consideration, on
such matters as these, than the beasts of the
field, and, on certain other Matters, with far
less consideration, But employers and favourers
of the "high handed " system generally ought
to be able to see that that time is passing away,
and that, perforce, they will have to accept
the new conditions brought by altered times.
Nobody wishes to see the authority required
to enforce all necessary duties of the workshop
rendered ineffeetive, but it is the interest of
everyone, cspecially tho worker, to see it
rendered reasonable and considerate. The
man placed in authority over working men

in England must have other characteristics
than those of a slave-driver, or his authority
will. be resisted and set aside. In this spirit
and no other the porters of the railway have
acted. As on Tuesday morning, after the
strike had been entered on, they wrote again
to the, authorities, asking if they could not
point out some method by which an amicable
settlement might be arrived at, and again
na reply was returned, the reasonableness of
the men being, no doubt, interpreted as weak-
ness.

It is said that the Company has secured men
enough to enable them, to carry on de traffio
efficiently. This of course, is the bright side
of the question; politio maybe, as a statement,
but laoking full truth as a fact. Those who
have Opportunities of knowing, assert that it
is very far indeed from being the case, and
that greatloss to the Company, and greatincon-
venieuce to the publio are still going on.
On inquiry too, it turns out that the reports
circulated concerning the bad conduct of the
men in seeking by overt acts. to injure the
company in a variety of ways are by no means
true. .The men have behaved themselves in a
quiet and.orderly manner, and:though it may
be difficult, if not impossible, to control every
individual in so largo a number, still the men
assert with confidence, and with the utmost
appearance of truth, that they have no know-
ledge whatever, and do not for a moment
believe that there is an atom of truth in the
statements spread broad-cask by the press,
and whieh in their concoction and circulation
were evidently designed, for their injury.
This battle may be lost by the men, though
at present they by no means think so. Pre-
suming such should he the case, however—
what then? Can the Directors believe it
possible to continue a system which has thrown
the men into such a state of decided revolt,
or do they imagine that these men will bow
their necks and pass submissively and con-
tentedly under the authority of a man against
whom, their feelings have been so bitterly
exalted? The' " point .of honour " is not
worth st!okitig for. Mr. O.REPTISII, if the
Directors think lit, may be placed. in some
situation iyht,re, his services may be available
for the Company, but where his conduct will
not provoke the hostility of those in connection
with whom he is put to, work. To keep him
where
.he is at present is to practically deny
the right of the men to -meet together for a
legitimate consideration of their interests; and
they will not submit to this, except under
compulsion, and then only whilst they are
organising their strength for a new struggle.
.The right to associate is, to woiking-men, a
sacred right. Private employers have had to
concede it,,. and railway companies, thotigh
apparently all-powerful, must submit to the
same fate, or they will have to prepare them-
selves for
.a battle in which every man who
lives by his labour, every man who sympathises
with the struggles of the down-trodden, every
man who believes that the principles of asso-
ciation arc preparing the way for power,
justice, and truer rights, will be on the side
of the Men.

articles.title: COLONIAL EXAMPLE.
articles.text:
A COLONIAL EXAMPLE.

INPonatATIoN has just been received from
the Cape of Good Hope that the Contagious
Diseases Act in force in that: colony has now
been completely repealed. The Bill finally
passed, the Legislature there on the 18th of
June. Your readers are probably aware that,
owing to the efforts of our Government,
booked up by its army and navy officials, the
Contagions Diseases Act has been established
in most of the colonies subject to British con-
tra It was one of the " blessings" t?)
which we conferred, along with Governor
EYRE'S rule,' on the happy; Island of Jamaica.
The history of the repeal now accomplished
of these Acts at the Cape of Geed Hope is
somewhat instructive at the present Moment.
It was not, found possible, owing to the
thrown in the way, to carry a Repeal
Bill there last session. The consequence was
that, when the Estimates came on for discus-
• sion, the Lower House, which there, as here,
has the power of the purse, refused to grant
the supplies for carrying out an Act of whose
principle they had already disapproved. This
Was a death-blow to the Acts, and practically
necessitated the passing this year of the pill
which has now finally passed for their repeal.
Your readers will by this time be aware that
a similar measure to stop the supplies for the
working of these Acts in this country' was
negatived last Monday in the House of 'Com-
mons. There is this difference between the
Lower House in Cale Town and the House of
Commons in this country, that the majority of
the Lower House there desired repeal, while
the majority of the House of Commons 'her.°
do not desire repeal. The Lower House there
represented the desire of the people of the
Cape; the. present House of Commons here on
this question, as on not a few others, does not
represent the wishes of the nation. The pre-
sent House of Commons is a " eltss" HOll5O
of Commons. We need to have shorter Par-
liaments, and working Men themselves in Par-
liament, for which end it seems to me that
perhaps the Most needed measure of electoral
reform is the payment of election expenses by
the electors and not by the candidates. -

There is one very signiacant point in the
debate in the Cap') Legislature to which I
wish to call your attention. " The chief op-
position to repeal," says the Cap° Argus,
"here, as in England, arose from ollicials,"
rind I observe that in the debate, one member,
in favour of the Acts, calls for remuneration

to the dotisters and surgeons employed under
them, wbo had been deprived of their way of
living by the vote of the Lower House. This
is always the way with centralized officialism,
and the claim for compensation is always sure
to be raised by any officials turned out of
office, however injurious their office may
have been to the public at large. This con-
sideration should make iatepayers and tax-
payers particularly careful against allowing a
centralized officialism, such as that which
carries on the Contagious Diseases Acts, to
arise in their midst, especially when it is
foisted upon them by a House of Commons
the backbone of which consists of men eon-
neoted with or actually, serving in the army
and navy. For army men of all others are
least capable of legislating for the civil com-
munity, and the fruit of their lucubrations we
at present see in their attempt to 'turn this
country against its will into a military
country by importing military centres--thos.e
centres of vice, immorality, and oppression—
into every part of the country.
JAMES STUART, M.A.,
Fellow and Assistant-Tutor of Trinity
College, Cambridge.

P.S.—Since writing the above I have just
received the division list on the vote on the
estimates. Seventy-six voted for Mr. JACOB
131LonT's motion to reject the sum for the acts
and. 142 voted against his motion. In the
majority I find the names of 16 army and. navy
officers, 3 viscounts, Words, 16 " sirs " and 16
" honnurables." Of the remainder a very large
number are members of the GoVernment, in-
cluding the Right Hons. GLADSTONE, BILUCE,
FonsTfat and Lowm, and the whole list bristles
with aristocratic names, while I search in vain
through the list for the names of any friends
of the people, whose names I find thickin the
minority.

articles.title: EMIGRATION.
articles.text:
EMIGRATION.

Transplantation is at the first a bad thing.
Many roots and fibres are torn in the process,
and it causes a violent shook whioh requires time
and a congenial soil to remove its effects. But
for many reasons it is often a necessity, and it
Produces a much higher avenge development than
can possibly he obtained without it. .
There are vast numbers of human plants with
ehance of air or sun in the presence of their
overlshadowing neighbours, and with scarcely a
hold in their native soil. Very many of them
slowly vogetatein the cold shade, with most of
their finer and better qualities starved out of
them-01(3y live despised and unnoted die. It needs
no argument to show that notwithstanding any
attendant evils, their circumstances woad be
vastly improved by judicious transplantation.
Could. English agricultunil labourers have been
thinned out by wholesale in this manner, it would
have been much better both for those that were
taken, and for those that were left.
Yet even these men are now proving themselves
something more than more vegetables to be trans-
planted or to be choked on their native soil, accord-
ing to the whims or fancied interests of other
organisms of a higher order than their own.
To the astonishment of. their lords and betters the
English :seas think and act; the stunted trees
transplant themselves; at their own pleasure:they
migrate, or ezigrate, or remain. The masters are
rather dismayed, but they are obliged to recognise
the fact, and to make terms with -those who till
lately, lived On. suffrance and in abject Submis-
sion. -

In reality, this attitude of the agricultural
labourers is the last °atom° of English emigra-
tion ; for, omitting 'intermediate causes, it is this
more than any, others that has primarily enabled
all grades of English working men to improve
their condition. Possibly, it is also this which
has long preserved the Throne, the House of Lords,
and our boasted English ConatitUtion.
Two hundred and fifty years ago emigration
began to draw off from old England considerable
numbers of persons of various classes, whose con-
dition here under the wise laws of our ancestors,
made them more or less dangerous to the then
existing order of things. In a few years it had
gained .a great impetus, and king, lords, and
squires, began to think that they should not have
a sufficient number of subjects left in tin old
country for them to govern. They, therefore,
adopted a course about as wise as the proverbial
one of sitting on the safety-valve to hold in the
steam—they stopped the emigrants by force-
-llad he not, like many others, been compelled to
remain in. England,
_Oliver Cromwell would have
been a comparatively insignificant and harmless

AUG. 3,187 g.

New England Puritan, rather than the ehief
instrument of the great Revolution that over-
whelmed King, Lords, and Commons. It is Tate
probable that the slow process of amelioration
which might have resulted from encouraged emi-
gration, would have spared us the Revolution and
its enormous waste of life and property, and
would also have secured more solid and per'
manent advantages to the people, than those which
resulted from that great convulsion.

Notwithstanding all the checks that colonization
received .from natural and artificial causes, the
political and social influence of the emigration of
the 16th, 17th, and 18th centuries was most
enormous. The year 1776 found the revolting
American colonies with a population of about
3,000,000, which was wholly the direct or indirect
result of emigration. The population of the old •
country at that time was about 7,000,000. The
emigration had been mostly from the middle
classes, with a sprinkling of labourers taken over
by their musters, and a considerable number of
superior mechanics who, even in those times, had
managed to save a little store for their dangerous
and rather expensive voyage. These people were
dangerous to the Governments of their ',Ames, fri?tu
the 'act that many of them knew and appreciated
the rights to which they were entitled, and which
had always been ignored or refused. When they
left, their places here were filled by others whose
condition was in consequence materially iuiproved,
and who, feeling this improvement, were much
less discontented subjects than they otherwise
would have been. Employers of 1 thour found
that they had in some measure to bid against the
attractions of the colanies, and the result was a
. ,
perceptible improvement in the material corelition
of: those who had even a reasonable chance of
stepping into the cast-off shoes of the more for-
tunate emigrants.
It is difficult to imagine the extent of the differ-
ence in the conlition of the working classes here,
if the ranks of the shopkeepers, mechanics, and
labourers had constantly become more and more
overstocked by the presence of these emigrants
and their descendants. Under wise laws there '
would have been room for four times the popula-
tion; but wise laws are very difficult to obtain even
now, and under such circumstances they would
have been impossible withotityevolution, and most
unlikely with it.
Some idea of what the resalt might have been
may be obtained from a glance at the condition of
France. That country was much wealthier and in
many respects more favoured than England. It
was also far more advanced in the arts ard
scienees. England's superiority was almost ,
entirely confined to the sea. But the superiority 1
of England at sea was a check upon emigration
from France, and about the middle of the eighteenth
century, the conquest of the great French colony of 4
Canada by England and her colonies virtually
destroyed it.

• In France, in the meantime, as the population
increased without an outlet, the working classes I
were more and more at the mercy of those abave
thum, and the share of the fruits of their labour
which they obtained became less and less. They I
could only live from hand to month, and combina-
tion for better pay would have been well nigh 4
impossible, even if there had been no terribly re-
pressive laws to insure abject submission. Their
misery reached the limit of endurance, and every-
one knows that the great French revolution was
the result, and that the vibrations of that terrible :
earthquake have not yet ceased to snake the
earth.

It would no doubt be very gratifying to our
self-love if we were able, advisedly and without
prejudice, to attribute to the English nation spe-
cial capacities for progrosaand self-government ;
but it is a fact that the circumstances in which
this country has been placed in regard to emigra-
tion, be had immensely more to do With our
precedence in these respects than our natioual
egotient is by any means dieposed to allow. If vcc
examine our political hietory without prejudice,
we shall find that our kings have seldom bees
very brilliant specimens of humanity. Our nobles
have n it often been gifted with remarkable poll'
tical foresight. The wisdom of our squirm:ell,
and the self-denial of our bishops and beneficed
clergy, have never been so great as to be Pr"
verbial among the other nvtions of the earth
;Until very ree3nl. times these have been our
governors; they have resisted all improvement°
which interfered in tho least with their pet pri'
vileges, and they have never yielded while there
was a chance of standing out.
If statesmanship consisted in low cheating, thee
the number of artful subterfuges oontrived by eur
ruhrs for the purpose of really withholding what
they found It absolutely necessary to concede in ar
pearanco, would certainly give to them a 'col

fair rank, and to us excellent reason to be proud of
their abilities.

Latterly, the middle classes have been the foun-
dations of power. They have always been a small
minority of our actual rulers, but they have made
and unmade our masters; and in all of those great
matters in wbich they could not be deceived, their
voice has been obeyed. They obtained this as-
cendancy by the active help and the moral support
of the working clasEes, without whose aid they
would have been powerless to obtain any really
substantial share in ihe Government; but they
have been in no greater haste to offer political
rights to the working men, than the individual
masters among them have been to advance wages,
from the mere spirit of fairness and without any
evident necessity.

T'ae greatest example that England can boast
of that unselfish regard for the right which is
the foundation of true political wisdom was
that afro' ded by the poor operatives of Lancashire,
in the earnest sympathy and moral suppmt which
they accorded to the people in the United States
in their death struggle with the overbearing slave
oligarchy of the South.

The real truth is that in England, as every-
where else, undue power brings an intense and
blind selfishness with it, and there is a moral
certainty that had not circumstances, the greatest
and most import tnt of which was the result of 'emi-
gration, so much strengthened the middle and lower
classes, that absolute resistance to their demands
was self-evident suicide, the ruling classes of
England, like those of France, would have conceded
nothing; and in the result we should have had no
reason to boast of English aptitude for self-
government.

Working men have now a very considerable
share of practical power. I' they could be gifted
with perfect wisdom and could insure the passing
and due enforcement or wise social, political, and
economical lawn, they might be able to make room
in old England, for twice the number of its present
population to live io prosperity and peace. But
at the beat such great improvements can only be
expected as the result of wise and long continued
efforts assisted by favourable circumstances, and
it behoves us to neglect nothing which is good in
itself and subsidiary to the grest end of moral and
material advancement. Free trade in articles
of food and raiment has been introduced with
advantage; and although we are by no means
so dependent upon emigration as we were alien
it was more difficult, let us have free trade in
human labour, the one great overwhelming
necessity of life. While we petfect our vuriou
trade organizations at home, let us use all neces-
sary means of getting perfect information from
abroad, and when we have the requisite knowledge
to work with, let us use the lever of a thoroughly
well-organised system of emigration, as one means
to help us, in achieving all that remains to be
accomplished at home.

THE RAILWAY SERVANTS.

THE LONDON AND, NORTH WESTERN.

Delegates representing about 1,000 men em-
ployed in the various London goods stations of the
London and North Western Railway Company
were a few days ago favoured with an interview
at Easton Station with Mr. Cawkwell, the general
manager, and Mr. Findlay, the goods manager
of the company, that they might present
him with a memorial of a somewhat extra-
ordinary character. It appears that some short
time since,'just after the railway servants' agitation
commenced, the London superintendent of the
company, Mr. G. Greenish, dismissed a clerk named
King, and a signalman named Tarbox, because,
as the men believe, they took part in the moVe-
went for an advance of pay and: shor:ening of
hours. This produced considerable dissatisfaction
amongst the men, which was increased when, as
they thought, the advances conceded by the
directors subsequently were unfairly distributed.
Hence the memorial signed by eight hundred men,
presented—the men having instructed their dele-
gates that they will leave their stations to a man;
unless the directors accede to Cleft requests, viz.:
—To remove Mr. Greenish from over them, and to
reinstate King and Tarbox.
Mr. Cawkwell and Mr. Findlay received the
delegates very courteously. They listened
attentively to the memorial, and promised to lay
it before the directors of the company, and that a
reply should be given in writing.
Subsequently, Mr. Baxter Langley received the
following letter from Mr. Cawk well :—" Man-
chester, July 246,
.1872.—Sir,—Your letter of
this date, with reference to a memorial from a
portion of the men employed by the London and
North Western Railway Company at their metro-
politan stations, was put into my hands just as I
was leaving town fur this place, and I lose no time
in giving you a reply. The request of the memo-
rialists—viz., that the Directors shouldiremove one
of their principal officers who has for a long time
served them faithfully and to their entire satisfac-
tion—is one which cannot be entertained, nor can
the Directors consent to leave such a question to
be decided by arbitration or to be dealt with by
anyone but themselves. In all matters of difference
between the Directors and any of their numerous
staff which are open to discussion they are always
prepared to deal with their views, and in the most
considerate manner, but the question now raised
is one which does not admit of diecussion.—Yours
faithfully, W. CAWIEWELL."
On Saturday the porters, about four hundred in
number, at the Broad-street goods station, struck
work, after receiving their week's wages. The
men at tlie Camden, Hayden-square, and Poplar

The statement which the men made in detail
goes far to confirm this gpneral view of the posi•

Greenish's part to remove the old bands, who

It is only fair to the hands who are out to say

defacing of labels and tampering with goods ready

The company have been able to secure all the

It is not correct, as reported, that the company
failed to deliver the dead meat or fish traffic. On
the contrary, it was dcal With at Camden without
the least inconvenience to the public. Nor has it

ThE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

KLNILIVORTII.

On Friday there was a large meeting of farm
labourers at the Castle Green, Kenilworth, to hear
arldret-ses from Mr. G. Potter aed Mr. Mi obeli, of
London, "one from the plough." The fifes and
diums, with their banners, went to the railway
station to escort tbe speakers to the green, with
a number of trade unionists who came by train, to
hear the well-known advocate of unionism, who
was also known to them as a native joincr Of
Kenilworth. Two waggons were drawn up on
the greeu as the platform, and there were about a
thousand persons present. On the motion of Mr.
H. Taylor, the general secretary of the National
Union, Mr. George Potter was called to the chair.
The Chairman spoke for au hour in advocacy of
the Union. He having referred to his following
the plough when a boy, proceeded to show that
the elevation of the farm labourers was a national
question, inasmuch as a half-starved peasantry
could not properly till the soil. He contended that
it would pay the farmer better to give good wages,
and that labour ought to share profits with
capital. He went into figures to show that the
rise in wages was not the cause of the dearness of
commodities. For instance, the coal miners had
only got an advance of 4id. a ton, who then got
the Gs. rise in price but the owners and dealers?
The labourers' wages had been stationary while
corn and meat had gone up in price, therefore this
charge of strikes being responsible for the rise in
commodities was absurd. He then pointed out
the power and utility of trades unions in enabling
a body of men to get that concession which a
single person could not get. Four unions alone
had in the last ten years paid £1,250,000 in relief
to members. He trusted the farmers would not
for their own sakes resort to extreme measures,
and predicted a prosperous future for agriculture
and England when farmers and men studied eaoh
other's interests. He urged all to join the ranks
of the rapidly extending National Union, which in
another twelvemonth, at the present rate of pro-
gress, would embrace every agricultural labourer
in Great Britain.

Mr. W. Taylor, chairman of the local committee,
proposed :
That this meeting deeply sympathires with the
long depressed condition of the agricultural
labourers of Warwickshire, and congratulates them
on the operations of the National Agricultural
Labourers' Union not only in this county, where it
originated, but throughout the eountry at large.
Mr. Wm. Denman seconded.

Mr. Geo. Mitchell, a marble merchant of London,
who as a Somersetehire p otighboy struck against
4s. a week, made a speech both amusing and
earnest. He expressed his determination to help
the Union to Ott utmost of his power.
Mr. H. Taylor made an energetic and argumen-
tative epeeeb, and was totowed by Mr. T. Conoli),
of Mr. Dixon's Canadian °Mee, 11, Adam-Art-et,
Westminster, who gave a glowing account of Cana-
dian setVers, and tffevel to send out any number
of farm Ithourers at £4 &. a head.
The resolution was, carried by acclamation, and
after vociferous cheering, the speakers were
escorted through the streets by the band playing
and the crowd cheering.

if they
.int.,,nded parting with it, they were the

Mr, B. Taylor (Peterborough) spoke next. He

nom the time of this agricultural movement

The chairman read letters of apology, contain-

THE NEW REFORM MOVEMENT.

The Committee appointed by certhin repre-
sentatives of the working classes for carrying
out the new nen min movement, to which
reference has been already made in our
columns, has forwarded us the following
official account of the meetings which have been
held and the programme which has been
adopted : _ _

Orn the evenings of June 19 and July 10 and
17, conferences of working men, presided over
by Mr. SAinuel Morley, M.P., wore held at
the Cannon-street Hotel. To these conferences
all who were known among the working
classes as taking an active part in nolitical
affairs were impartially invited, and of 78
invited about 60 attended and took part in the
proceedings. As the result of these meetings
the following programme and address were
agreed and areal to Without any dissentient
voices, not hiea dozen of those present having
left the room before the vote was taken. A
. committee
,was chosen at the third meeting
charged with the following duties :-1. To
print and circulate the programme throughout
the Country with an address recounting the
circumstances under which it was drawn up,
denying that it. is intended to serve
existing party purposes, or that it is
designed to supersede any existing as-
sociations, reserving the right of those
who sign it, to maintain and propagate
more advanced views, and inviting working
men to signify their approval of the platform.
2. To call a representative meeting of the
various political and social organizations in the
Metroplis, with a view of obtaining their support.
It was also resolved that a meeting should be
called of all those who give in their adhesion
—such meeting to elect a general eduncil, who
shall urge upon the constituencies the ad-
vantages of selecting for themselves, as
candidates for the next Parliament, men who
accept the platform; also that
,such council
shall appoint an Executive charged with the
duty of carrying out their instructions. A so-
called " authentic " report having appeared in
some of the daily journals, which is very incorrect
as regards the programme and as regards tho
proceedings at the conferences, the committee
append the programme and address. No
persons attended the Meeting as representing
societies, and it was not guaranteed nor
understood that the expenses attending the
movement weuht be provided by any individual
or association.

TO TIIE WORKING CLASSES OP TIIE UNITED
KrNODOI4.

Fellow Working Mn,—Oa the evenings of
June 19 and July tO ansl 17, conferences repre-
senting the progressive sections of working men in
London, were held at the Cannon-street Hotel,
414 after considerable discussion the following
programme was agreed upon. In its adoption we
have endeavoured to keep in view two things,
viz., what is necessary and what is possible' and
for the sake of what is now possible we have
omitted much that is necesslry, but we trust that
our doing so will not prevent your thorough union
with us. Its initiation and adoption are not the
result of any design to serve existing party pur-
poses, or to supersede any existing associations,
but are the outgrowth of national wants and con-
victions. Those who give their adhesion to this
programme reserve to themselves the right to
maintain and propagate more advanced principles
which they may hold. We believe the programme
to be one upon which at I:sincere and honest reformers
may unite, and that it is not only practical, but
necessary, fur the following rea4ons :--1. :-Because
the old Liberal programme is well nigh exhausted,
and it Is time we had another which shal combine
social with political reform. 2. Because we be-
lieve that untOis some well-defieed and progressive
Platform is agreed 'upon, at the next general
°lotion it will be difficult to distinguish between
real and sham reformers. 3. Because the pro-
gramme, used as a test of a candidate's profesrdons,
will help to keep out of the next House of Com-
mons tricksters and shallow politicians of any
class and enable electors to distinguish between
-
men of profeszions and men of principles.

articles.title: STRIKES IN GERMANY.
articles.text:
THE STRIKES IN GERMANY.

The difficulty of getting workmen still con-
tinues in an alarming degree, and strikes of
greater or less importance occur. The most
serious at present is that at the coalpits of
Essen. It seemed from the amiunts Of June 27
that it was like to pass off quietly, the Work-
men resuming their labour on the old terms,
but the accounts, more recently are leas favour-
able. Some Social Democrat tramps have got
amongst them, and working hand in hand with
the religious fret to be found in most minds in
Catholio districts it is feared the storm will
not, blow over till it has raged itself weary.
I do not mean to say that the clerical influence
in creating dissatisfaction among the pitmen is
direct. But proofs are present that the plan of
the general strike has been originated in those
circles over which Catholic clergy possess most
influence. For a whole month past a growing
excitement has been remarked among the
Catholic miners. It is observable amongst
those people (especially when they have had a
glass 1) that they have lately indulged in a
most contemptuous tone towards the Empire,
the Emperor, and the Chancellor, and their
meetings. Instead of canvassing their own
affairs, as seems most natural, they inveigh
against Bismark, as if he were the individual
who was refusing them higher wages. A
resolution was formed on the part .of the
officials to take no miner for the space of four
weeks. The name Essen Will remind hundreds
of Alfred Krupp and his great gun. His enor-
mous establishment is in rssen, but no strike
has taken place there. He has thought fit,
however, to issue a very characteristic
document to his min, of which I think it worth
to give a short resume. IL addresses himself to,
''the workmen in
,the oast-steel works :"
"Forty-five years ago I Stood in the ranks of a
low workmen amid the beginnings of these
works, my father'S heir, Then a man earned
his four and sixpence a-week. Fur fifteen
years 1 gained exactly so muoli as to pay my
men, and for myself only the consciousness of
having fulfilled my duty. I have kept pace
with the graduil change in the general social I
relations, and have voluntarily increased my,
men's wages' adding One useful arrangement
and desirable comfort after the other, and
dwellings by the thousand. When business
was slack I have continued to employ my
men, and never turned off a good hand.
There are many still living who min tell what
was done for them in 1848. The losses
brought by the years of war are known to Our-
selves. And who can calculate the losses by
the present lack of coal ? The establishment
hassprospered on mutual confidence. I know
I possess and deserve yours, therefore I address
you in, these words. Before even I have
occasion to complain, I warn you against
accusing toe of unfaithfulness, and of listening
to what wandering discontented spirits may'
pour into your ears." He prOceeJs to tell
thein that if they maintain their present bear-
ing all will be conducted liberally as heretofore,
and every
.workman, after his stated years of
labour, enjoy his pension in his own house as
nowhere else in the world. But if they attempt
to coerce him in his own dominions(he has
above ten thousand men), he reminds them the
works may pass as a joint-stock concern into I
other hands. There is something heroic in the
address, but I should think rather calculated
to fret excitable spirits than sooth them.

and a verdict for the plaintiff, with nominal

THE GOVERNMENT AND THE
FACTORY OPERATIVES.

On Monday two important deputations
Waited upon Mr. Bruce at the Home Office—
the one to urge upon ' the Government
the necessity foradopting Mrl Mundella's Bill
for the shortening of the hours of labour of
women and children in factories; .the second
to urge that, on the contrary, no such legisla-
tion is needful, and that any such restriction
of the hours of work would be injurious to
the English. trade. The first deputation con,
sisted of both employers and employed, and
was beaded by Lord Shaftesbury, the Hon.
E. Ashley, Mr. A. G. Mundella, M.P.; Mr.
It, N. Phillips, 'M.P., Mr. It. Shaw, ALP., Mr.
C. S. Parker, M.P., Mr. Wm. Then (of Fison
and Foster, Bradford), Mr. J. White (Brad-
ford), Mr. J. Brandwood (Blackliurn), Coun-
cillor J. Beads. (Blackburn), Mr. Aaron
(Bay), Mr., W.,Leigh (Nlancliester), and -Mr.
Phillip Gfant, and 'operatives from East Lan-
eashire' Dundee, Oldham, Bolton, and Stook-
port,and were dressers, weavers, and spinners.
When the deputation first entered Mr. Bruce
had net arrived, in town, and Mr. Winter-
botham undertook to convey to Mr. Bruce all
that was said.
Mr. Mundella said lie had bean asked to
introduce the deputation, he being in charge
of the Bill for shortening thehours of labour of
women and children, and those present were
equal numbers of employers and employed.
The deputation asked .the sympathy of the
Government for the nine hours movement as
embodied in the Bill, and said that for the
health, recreation,,and education of the people
the time had now come when the Factory
Acts should be brought into the limits so far
as they affected women and children, Of what
were now the ordinary labour hours of the
country.

Mr. P. Grant then pointed out that in Lan-
cashire Many of the trade worked only 51
hours a week, and none more than 51s, and
that the comforts of home were lost to the
men who worked at these other trades by the
women of the house Ring out to work before
the men and returning home after them at
night. He read letters from Mr, W. 1.
Romaine Callender and other millowners in
support of the deputation's views.
Lord Shaftesbury spoke of the great desire
of the people to have the interposition of Par-
liament in place of striking, and he hoped
that Parliament would not allow this law-
abiling position to go for nothing.
Mr. T. Birtwhistle, an operative from East
Lancashire, described the effects of the
"singing" and "steaming" operations upon
the health of the operatives; and he entered
upon a variety , of statistics to show that the
East Lancashire operatives were much shorter
lived than inhabitants of large towns in
general.
Mr. Middleton, of Dundee, for the Scotch
jute works, spoke to the effect that the nine
hourEi were greatly wanted there for the
women, the work being exceedingly heavy,
and the number of women employed very large
as doinpared with the men.
• Mr. Fison (employer) spoke as to the work
in the woollen trade, and said that whenever
some woollen factories he never saw so attenu-
ated a set of people in his lrfe as the workers.
Re considered that the application of the
operatives for the shorter hours was based on
just grounds, and that their cause was as
strong and just as their opponents was weak
and unjust. Moreove.,r, the people deserved
the concession they asked for tire noble atti-
tude they had taken.

Mr. Winterbotham spoke of the necessity
for inquiry befere any course was. adopted by
the Government, ana promised to lay the sub-
ject before Mr. Bruce,. and he agreed that the
law-abidingness of the operatives entitled them
to every consideration.
In regard to the word "inquiry," one of
the deputation said the operatives would not
Lave the matter shelved under such a plea, and
Mr. Winterbotharn said he did not tnean a com-
mittee or anything like that.
Mr. Bruce then (tame in, and he apologised
for his absence. An outline of the arguments
was presented to him, and Mr. Shaw, M.P.,
addressed him and stated that as the machinery
now caused 30 and 50 per cent. more work to
he done by the same number of hands, it was
apparent that there must be a greater btiain
upon the people than before,
Lord Shaftesbury, in answer to Mr. Bruce,
said that he was most certainly in favour of
the proposed amendment to the Factory Acts.
Mr. ltruce said he %would undertake during
the vacation to make inquiry to see if the
lessened hours were needed, for if they wre
necessary for the health of woman and chil-
dren they ought to he adopted no matter what
• were the eilents upon. trade. •
The depot akin then withdrew.
The second deputationWt from the York-
shire Associstion of Mill 0 inupiers; and was
iiitrAnced by L'ird Fred,riek theeurlish,
• xk.A., alia Cu'ouel AlZroyd, M.P. The mem-
bers of the dli.itiltioa addressed Mr. Itrii2o at

.against the proposal to
shorten the 11 .urs of will labour for women
and children. They said that the mills 114)%1
only ran 5g hours a week, and it was under
cowideratiou to give another hour. The

agitation they .dealared was the work of the
overlookers, who were paid weekly wages,
and would have as much for nine as for ten
hours. The deputation declared that the
women and children were not overworked,
and were contented. The deputation asked
the. Government to institute an inquiry into
the hours, wages; and other matters in foreign
countries, so as to compare with our own

Air. Bruee said that. the inquiry for which

stituted; but wivitever might be the effect of
shortened hours of labour upon trade was,
after all, a secondary matter, for the health
and education of the people would he the first
consideration.

Many tinestions were asked of members of'
the deputation, and the 'conversation which
ensiled was a long one, and lathe course of it
Colonel Akroyd said that women in factories

domestic women.

articles.text:
THE SUNDAY OPENING OF MUSEUUS.

A deputation representing the Working
Men's Lord's-day Rest Association waited
upon the Right lion. W. E. Firster, at the
Education Department, on Tues lay afternoon,
with the Object. of urging the Government to
resist the agitation for the opening of the
Bethnal-green and other mussinni on Sun-
days. The deputation was headed by Lieut.-
Colonel Roxburgh, Major Ditness, Mr. M. T.
Braithwaite, Mr. V. C. P. Young, and Mr.
Charles Hill, the secretary of the association;
and the members were introduced by Mr. E.
Baines, M.P. It was submitted by. the
different speakers that the proposed step, be.'
sides violating the religious character of the
Lord's-day, would lead at the outset to a large
aggregation of Sunday labour, and. ultimately
to the opening of all places of amusement.
The whole question was involved in the
decision of the Government with regard to the
East London Museum, the demands for the
opening of which it was stated did not rot:et-01
.from the working-class body, but a few in-
terested individuals. The great majority
favoured the views of the, association, and it
would ill become the Government to act in
opposition to the expressed feelings of the
country, and especially of the working classes.
Mr. Forster Observed that the deputation
assured him positively, that the .working class
body was opposed. to the opening of these
museums on Sunday; 'but, on the other band,
he was also informed in equally positive lan-
guage to the contrary effect by.a counter ease-
eiation to their own, but also professing to
represent the working classes; therefore the
matter must be weighed upon its real merits.
Regarding the main questionr.he could only
refer them to what had been stated in the
House of Commons, which was that the Go-
vernment, having reg ird to the. present state
of public business, w.,re not prepared to sanc-
tion the opening of museums on Sundays.
Unless a decided feelit.g was manifested in its
favour they would not make the alteration.
There were, however, arguments for the Sun-
day opening, one of whieh was that a desirable
and benefiCial competition with the public-
houses would result. Still there would be
some danger in adopting the course, and it
behoved Parliament and the cabinet, before
embarking upon it, to very carefully cousider
the question. In reference to the East-end
Museum, the only steps taken had
been that, finding same of the upper classes
visited the institution on Sundays, the prac-
tice was put a stop to. Whatever opinions he
might individually bold—and they were not
in exact accordance with the views of the
deputation--:-he assured them that nothing
would be done without due consideration and
a careful estimate of public opinion. The de-
putation then thanked the right. hon. gentle-
man and withdrew.

SATURDAY, AUGUST 3, 1872.

AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS' WAGES.
IN another column will be found a letter
from lir. C. H. NEVILE, of Thorney, Notting-
hamshire, commenting on an article of ono
which appeared on the 13th ult.' relative to
the Bishop of PETERBOROUGH'S condemnation
of outside agitators, who, as he
.said, were
stirring up strife between the farmers and
their labourers. In that article the question
of wages was but referred...to incidentally, nor
was it stated or left to be inferred that the
general wages of farm labourers throughout
the country were nine, ten, or eleven shillings
a week only—although such is most assuredly
the case in extensive districts in England.
We know as well as he] does that wages vary
in different
.parts of the country, and inas-
much as our remarks bore reference ;neces-
sarily to those places where the present
agitation was going on, the low:wages of the
worst paid counties could only be alluded to
by us. /We assure Mr. NEVILE that we haie
gone very carefully over Parliamentary re-
ports and other documents iwith the view of
ascertaining the real state of the case as
regards the wages of agricultural labour, and
we can only come to the conclusion that,
all things counted in, from eleven to thirteen
shillings per week covers everything in the
agrieultural districts proper. We know that
those districts of the country where manu-
factures are carried on, labour in the fields
rates higher, though a shilling or tWo as a
rule would settle the difference.
We wish to avoid exaggeration of any kind,
but we do not desire to be hoodwinked. We
are willing, in dealing with this question of
wages in the rural districts, to be guided hy
authority, bat we are anxious that the
authority to which we refer should be above
suspicion of any kind. It is, therefore, we
turn to official records, and the first we cite is
Mr. ALFRED AUSTIN, at one time "Special
Assistant Poor Law Commissioner." Writing
in his official capacity, he gives the wages of
Wiltshire as ranging between Bs. and 10s. per
week, on an average 9s. 6d.; in Dorsetshire,
us, per week ; in Devonshire, slightly higher;
in Somersetshire the labourer is worse off than
in Wiltshire. In Lincolnshire, Mr. DENNI-
sox, also "Assistant Commissioner," puts the
wages at 1 is. per week; whilst Sir F.
DOYLE, another "Assistant Commissioner,"
makes the following remarks relative to the
East Riding of Yorkshire ;—" I advert to a
mode of paying wages in 'the East Riding, of
which I cannot but disapprove. The labourers
arc fed in the farmhouses, and have a certain
proportion of wages deducted to pay for their
meat. This proportion (Is. per day), if we
take wages at 13s. a week, which was as high
as they were in January, amounts to six-
thirteenths of the man's entire income from
work ;:so;that, setting aside her husband's food:
half and a fraction of his earnings is all that
a woman has with which to confront
the rest of life, her food, that of her children,
tinheedicraelnt a
totfen
dt haen
cec, o titlaagvee,
af ,
ll to eblieo
pro-
vided out of a sum only just larger than
is retained, for the bare meat and drink of en
individual labourer."
Need we remind Mr. NEVILB that in the
eases tried within the last few days in Dor-
chester and elsewhere the wages proved 0
subject of engagement between the prosecutors
and their labourers were ou this saws
wretchedly meagre scale; and, perhaPsf he
may be interested to know that in the rimes
of July 30th, Mr. MECHI, writing hopefal
of harvest and wages in his own rieighbotir7
hood, tells us that harvest wages htwe b°6l.
agreed upon at £6 fez' forkr weeks,

The whole of this may be pure invention.
Posen')ly Mr. NEVILE in a post Or two will
inform us it is so. His figures, taken from the
liWrwers' Chronicle of July Ist, give 15s.
as the lowest, and 18s. as the highest, run-
ning up for certain work to 7s. a day, and in
harvest time from £2 to .£4 per week.
Clearly there is a terrible delusion somewhere.
If the common opinion is correct, Mr. NEVILE
must have somehow or other got into a magni-
ficent fool's paradise. But if he sees things
in their right light, we can suggest to him and
to other farmers interested, a way out of the
present difficulty; and though we do this as
"outsiders," we hope ho will pardon us on
the ground of the profit of our suggestion.
Fifteen shillings a week is, as a rule, the
labourer's demand, and our hint is that the
farmers should at once accede to this
demand, and keep in their own pockets the
large overplus they are at present paying
them. If they act thus the labourers will be
satisfied by having their demands complied
with, and the farmers will make a handsome
profit by the compliance.
We imagine, however, that Mr. NETILE
must have made a mistake; the neighbour-
hood he inhabits cannot be actually in Eng-
land. It, no doubt, floats above the earth
like Laputa, and the people lie on the sunny
slopes of the hills and enjoy life as they did
in the Golden'Age. The shepherds pipe and
dance in true pastoral style, crowned with oak
leaves, and the innocent damsels adorned with
wreaths of flowers frisk with them on smooth
lawns kept ever verdant by purling streams
in which the beauties of the heavens are con-
stantly rtfleoted. We think Mr. NEVILE
should take his bearings afresh, and find Out
exactly where ire is, and inform the agricul-
tural labourers outside how to get there. El-
dora.da, Utopia, or the City of the Sun, must
be poor places compared to it.

Self-glory glistens o'er all that's there!
The trees, the flowers have a jaunty air;
The well-bred wiud in a whisper blows,
The snow, if it snows, is couleur de rose,
The falling fountain a titter fall,
And the sun looks simpering down on all.

Why should Canon GTRDLESTONE and Mr.
ABM cast their shadows into this happy land.
Let the 6 6 Thirdborough "be fetched, and the
parish stocks called into requisition. Let alt
such croakers be punished. Everything is
right in this best of all possible worlds.

Come knit hands, and beat tho ground
In a light fantastic round.

TIIE PRICE OF MEAT.

Of a material reduction in the price of
meat, the prospect does not seem very bright.
The only defence that consumers have is, either
to turn vegetarians or to put themselves up on
short rations of beef and mutton. Cattle plague,
according to Mr. FORSTER, exists at Hamburg.
The order, therefore, which had allowed
cattle from Schleswig-Holstein to come in
without slaughter at the port of landing has
been cancelled. Sheep also from Germany, as
well as cattle, must be so disposed of. Wo
must wait, therefore, until the Germans can
"stamp out" the disease. Precautions have
been taken at Hartlepool and Newcastle to
prevent the infection from reaching English
cattle. The Senate of Lubeck have like-
wise adoptel measures to stop diseased
cattle or their. hides from passing by that
channel. We observe in connection with this
subject, that Mr. JAMES HOWARD, Member for
Bedford, has given notice, that with a view
to increase the productiveness of farms in
Great Britain, particularly in the supply
of meat, he will, early, in the session of
1873, "bring in a Bill to extend and legalise
agricultural tenant-right in this island.

articles.title: PETITIONS TO PARLIAMENT.
articles.text:
PETITIONS TO PARLIAMENT.

OUR readers will have noticed from the pro-
ceedings in the House of Commons a few days
ago, a special report, presented by Mr.
CITA.BLES FORSTER, complaining of a breach of
privilege on the subject of public petitions, If
any feeling was experienced on the question at
all, it was one of wonder that such a report
occurs so seldom. All who know anything of
petitions, of the manner in will& they are got
up, of the means by which signatures are pro-
cured, and of the fashion in which they are
received and finally dealt with by the House
of Commons, must have felt long ago assured

that this practice, which is popularly suppossed*
to supply ri direct channel of communication
between the people and its representatives,
must be considerably modified. .
The petition in question was from the work-
ing men of Manchester, and was presented by
Mr. SEEJTANT SIMON, he being selected by the
promoters because he was a working man's re-
presentative ; and in justice to Mr. Simorr we
give the exact particulars.
A deputation of working men holding high
office and positions in trade and friendly so-
cieties, waited upon Mr. &amis., and asked
him to present a petition, which would con-
tain 60,000 signatures of working men,
praying that the . hours of opening and
closing public-houses should be the same in
the country as in the metropolis. They stated
various reasons, and• assured him that it was
purely a working class movement, in proof of
which they wished the Bill before the House
to pass as it was. They also informed Mr.
Srmex that the petition would come from
Manchester, Salford, and the district. Mr.
SmoN asked why it was that they did
not apply to, their own members. They
gave their reasons, which need not be men-
tioned here; but said that it was the
general wish' that Mr. Simerr himself
should present the petition. Upon being
asked why they selected him, they said,
"Why, you are well known as a
barrister on our circuit during the assizes
for so many years, and, as member for
Dewsbury, we look upon you as a working
man's representative." Mr. SIMON inquired
how the petition was being prepared, and
how the signatures were being obtained.
They assured him that the greatest care was
being taken in the manner of obtaining the
signatures, and that he might rely upon their
genuineness. Mr. SIMON warned them of the
consequences if the signatures were got sur-
reptitiously, or if they should turn out not to
be genuine. He also again expressed a wish
not to present it, and told them that it would
weaken the force of the petition when it was
seen that it was presented by a strange mem-
ber, and not by one of their Own. They still
urged him to present it; and ha then said, "I
must, before consenting, speak to the Members
for Manchester and Salford." He did so. He
spoke to Sir T. BASLEY, Mr. ,TAbon Bluant,
Mr. COWLEY, and Mr. Cuumn. Mr. BIBLEY
he could not get at at the time. Mr. SIMON
explained the circumstances here stated to the
above-named gentlemen, and received their
assent and thanks for his courtesy.
After this he presented the petition. It is
not usual for members to examine petitions
beyond,seeing as, to certain formalities, and
no member could be expected to give up press-
ing public work to look through a petition 107
yards long, containing ifimards of 69,000
signatures.

Mr. JACOB BRIGHT said in the House that
the hon. member for Dewsbury had been most
unjustly attacked, but he had done nothing
more than his duty in presenting the petition,
and throughout had acted in a thoroughly
friendly manner. '

Sir W. LAMSON also said that no blame
could be attaohel to the hon. member for
Dewsbury, and that he
,had acted in the most
honourable manner.

The right of petition is a sacred one, and
it must not be supposed that because a
member presents a petition that he is in
favour with its object, or is friendly to its
promoters. Mr. &mom appears to have gone
beyond his desire in order to serve some men
of Manchester, whose duty it is now to come
forward and cover him from any appearance
of participation in the affair.

articles.title: PROSECUTION OF LABOURERS.
articles.text:
PROSECUTION OF LABOURERS.

Filen different parts of the country accounts
have appeared in the papers of prosecutions
and convictions of farm labourers, for having
left their employers before their term of en-
gagement had expired. These are important
facts, and require the immediate attention
of the Leamington Union, that some rule of
action may be laid down on the subjeot appli-
cable to the country generally. There can be
no doubt whatever that in the agricultural
districts hiring by the year is pretty generally
the custom I and wherever mach hirings have

taken place, and have been fairly carried out
by the employers, good faith on the part of
the men in fulfilling their share of the bargain
should be urged and maintained. Only the
agents of the Leamington Union should be
instructed to make inquiry into every case,
with the view of finding out whether the con-
ditions of the engagement on the other side
have been carried out in their integrity, and
where any default has taken place on the part
of the farmer, every necessary legal step
should be taken to drag his victims from his
grasp.

In addition to this, every ease7.should be
brought under review by some competent
lawyer for the purpose of discovering whether
the decision of the magistrate, and the punish-
ment inflicted are strictly legal, and upon
every fitting opportunity appeal should be
made to the higher courts. Everybody must
know how scant justice will be for poor
labourers when farmers and country gentle-
men appeal to county magistrates against
refractory labourers; and; therefore,, as the
sympathy of the country is much in
favour of the poor labourer, every
energy should be strained to place at
his disposal the best possible means
of defence. In this great:struggle, it is neces-
sary the labourers should not place themselves
in the wrong by violating any engagement
into which they have deliberately entered.
But, on the other hand, -when the ignorance
of the masses of our labourers is taken into
account, as well as the one-sidedness, of the
judges' in our rural districts, too much
watchfulness cannot be exorcised for the pro-
tection of the weaker party.
It must be remembered thatlif the battle be
rightly fought by the men not under engage-
ment,.it will be won for all, if not at the
moment, at farthest as soon as the term of
engagement has been reached by those hired
for the year. Their bondage has lasted along
time. They have journeyed patiently over a
rough and weary road, and they must not,
now that a cheering light has been flung
across their path, allow their impatience to
delay their progress. The. day of their de-
liverance is truly at hand, but they must be
patient and law•-abiding, or, like drowning
men struggling for life, they may frustrate
the best efforts made for their rescue.

If the farmers and county magistrates
would listen to our voice, we would advise
them earnestly not to strain the law in their
determination to extort their pound of flesh.
Their yoke has been heavy for many weary
years._ They have left the poor labourer
nothing but his over-toiled awl exhausted
frame, and there may be danger in continuing
the torture after the hope of release has en-
tered the poor man's heart. We arc anxious
to see the change now taking place made in
peace. We know it will be hotter for all
parties should this be the ease. The incidents
of these trials show how galling the servitude
of the field is. Out of nineteen labodrers
brought before the Magistrates at the
Shire Hall, Dorchester, the following
case, stated on evidence, was not, as will be
seen, the worst of the lot. Jonzi OLD, a shep-
herd, had
.agreed to work for Mr. &moms for
twelve months at 103. per week with perquisites.
thus one ton of coal per annum; say ad. a week
at the outside; twenty shillings more for extra
work during each of the two seasons of harvest
and lambing, which would be a fraction over
NI. a week ; and 12 gourds of potatoes, the
value of which our agricultural experience
does not enable us to estimate, but if we put
them down at a guess as is. per week, we
shall find that this man's income, stated fully
in court, made up of wages and much lauded
"perquisites," amounts to 13s. id. 'Another
ease given was not so favourable. HENRY
TRINICEL, a carter and his two sons, earned
respectively the father Bs. per week, and the
two sons 13s. between them.

One way or another we shall get the whole
truth out. We shall know on their own
testimony in our, courts of law what
wages British farmers pay their labourers,
and in this way we shall also come to under-
stand the slough of misery and suffering out
of which springs the grandeur and greatness
of England's nobility and, landed gentry,
The subject is a dangerous one to tough, but

it cannot be left alone any longer with safety.
For good or evil the whole thing will have to
be stirred up from the bottom, and if our
farmers, and squires, and nobles—ignobly
thriving on the misery of others—know their
duty instead of howling denials, they will
enter on a work of reform which must be
carried out either .with their assistance or
against the strongest opposition they may
offer.

To state the facts settles the question.
They cannot resist by argument, and even the
most solid and profound lying will not answer
at a time when personal observation may be
so easily- brought to bear on the subject.

THERE are some few questions whioh may
be asked in a cursory way through the
columns of a newspaper, but which cannot be
answered satisfactorily except by careful en-
quiry into a large number of facts, many of
which arc not very easy to be got at. 'Work-
ing men are interested in watching with great
care the changes going on around them, and
in keeping strict record of their character, so
far, at least, as they are connected with
alterations in the condition of labour. There'
ought to be in the public mind a very clear
understanding as to whether the greatly en-
hanced price of nearly every commodity which

articles.text:
OVER LEGISL kTION.

TitguE are cants of all kinds and colours,
from those which peep through the Sleeves of
bishops to those which we daily meet amongst
men of the world, and whickdeoeive us by the
straightforward simplicity of their looks.
There' is one now walking about in a very
simple and modest garb, and its cry to the
crowd is that "over legislation" should be
be avoided. 11r., VERNoN HARcounT intro-
duced it at Oxford a few nig:its since, and
since then it has done service in certain of our
Liberal newspapers, and has been paraded and
praised as the newest, truest, and most im-
portant discovery of modern times. "A. ses-
sion or two ago," says Ur. H kncouirr, "a
gentleman introduced a Bill to compel railway
companies to provide feet warmers in :their
carriages; and he was only, the day before,
standing at the bar at the House of Lords,
listening to the discussion of a Bill for the
purpose of putting down acrobatic perforin-
Races."

Now what does this, and a great deal more
that has been said and might be added,
amount to? If it was unnecessary legislation
It was most assuredly "over legislation,' but
in itself it might be quite as small, and at the
same time very necessary and useful. The
turtling of keys and locking in of railway
passengers was quite as trivial, but it bad to
be interfered with. Very petty things have
In them frequently very important bearings
on the comfort, security, and welfare of the
general community, whilst very great things,
by magnitude of appearance, may be of far less
importance.
What Mr. Ilmientrat means, we apprehend,
is " foolish " legislation. tenet he rebukes in
the tendency of our legislation is foolish,
absurd, ridiculous, preposterous, unreason-
able, irrational, simple, silly, unwise, vain,
trifling, nonsensical, imbecile, weak, peurile,
rash, incautious, hasty, precipitate legislation.
We give him the advantage Of a handful of
synonymes that lie may not oonfine himself to
one word the next tinie he takes this question
up. "Over legislation" means all this, and
cannot mean anything else, unless it means
knavish legislation, which, it may be admitted,
is by no means an impossible thing.
Besides, this is not a teadeaoy of the pre-
sent age, and whether it be so or not, we have
to thank our legislators for giving it scope in
the nation's Parliament. We have foolish
legislation because we have foolish legislators,
and for no other reason in the world. We
have peddling and meddling; Bills brought in
and paged through Parliament because those
who make our laws are so mmy of them
peddlers and meddlers. True statesmanship
will trace an important national influence of
the good. or of the oil kind from a most
trivial circumstance, and lift or depress the
nation by the passinl.,, of a sin al enactment,
or the trifling alteration in some old mis-
ohievous law, whilst members of Parliament,
who, for the most part are anything but
statesmen, wouli, in their fondest tones of

contempt, call such proceedings, over-legis-

talon."

If Mr. HARCOURT, and those who act with
him, will save us from meddling and ped-
dling, and cobbling, and tinkering legislation,
and frothy fuss of a thousand kinds in the
Honso of Commons, they will save us from
" over-legisdation." If they will struggle
with energy to get good men and
good measures into the House, they
will do something to rescue that assembly
from the charge to which it is now fairly
open, and the country will gain by their
efforts. But if we are only to have disquisi-
tions against what is called " over-legisla-
tion." we shall end where we began. Or,
perhaps, some day finish with .a
Revel Com-
mission sent into the country to find out how
men usually scratch their heads, with the
view, of passing a law regulating the times,
the seasons, and the manner in which that
pleasant operation shall be indulged in. The
term "foolish legislation" we have no objec-
tion to, simply because it is only "over-
legislation," because it is foolish. This old
word is plain, but it is better than that
which has been substituted for it, as it does
not cover a cant nor carry with it the appear-
ance of a discovery.

MR. CLADSTO.)iE AT THE MANSION

HOUSE.

LOUD Marc) it's dinners are, as a rule, bountiful
enough to put those who partake of them into
good humor with themselves as well as with
the world generally. .After feeding abundantly,
it is only reasonable that men should try to
speak pleasantly, and, even though the political
road be rough and miry, it is sound policy
only to see for a moment those parts that lie
level and pleasant in the sunshine.
Still, when Mr. GLADSTONE spoke of capital
and labour, of employers and employed in his
speech at the Mansion House the other day,
he scorned .us to have gone unneces-
sarily beyond this in praising the spirit in
which quarrels between employers and em-
ployed had been eonducted in the past, and
in hoping that the same Spirit would prevail in
times to come, he uttered what could hardly
be the true conviction of his mind. Every-
one who wishes to see the industry of the
country flourish, will join in him in the hope
that a good and kindly spirit may prevail in
the future. We require it, and must have it;
but, instead of being like -what has existed in
the past, it is deArable it may be as unlike
that as possible. The old strike weapon has
not broken in the hands of the workmen; it
is, in fact, more potent than over. Still, it
should be flung away as an instrument of
almost unmixed mischief, as a painful and
costly mode of attaining an object, much
more easily and speedily gained by peaceable,
friendly arbitration. The more modern, but
more senseless lock-out, upon which employers
rely, must also be abandoned. It is even a
more stupid method of fighting than by strike,
but these methods combined are so utterly
unreasonable and mischievous, that Mr. GLAD-
sToNE, instead of referring to them with
implied satisfaction, ought to have spoken
strongly and boldly out against them.
Every man whose business or whose duty it
I is to address the public should do so as far as
possible in words of plain truth, as the plain
truth in this case is that all disputes between
employers and employed should be arranged
by friendly arbitration. A recommendation
of such a kind coming from the lips of Mr.
GLADSTONE could not buthave a good effect, and
it is a pity that he preferred a bit of smooth flat-
tery—laeking the recommendation of truth—
to a few honest words which, if spoken at the
present moment might, in their immediate
as well as in their ultimate effect, have done
much good to the two rival industrial interests
now at war. •

Another point touohed in the Mansion
House speech requires notice: When referring
to the matters at present in dispute between
England and Atherton, and complimenting
Englishmen on the "prudence and patrioti-m"
which on their part restrained unfriendly
criticism, it might hare been intimated that it
WilEI a vulgar patri.tisrn without prudence
during the late war in America, which made
the situation in which "prudence" has own o

to he ranked as a patriotism. After dinner
compliments aro easy and pleasant, but a little
more prudent thoughtfulness at all hours of
the day on all matters of grave national im-
port, would, beyond all question, render much
soft after-dinner small-talk altogether un-
necessary. Mr. GLADSTONE is 110 doubt a
master in this as in all other kinds of talk.
But HERCULES with the distaff is not an
edifying spectacle, however mush lie may
surpass his fellow spinners in drawing out his
thread.

POLITICAL AND SOCIAL REFORMS.
For forms of government let fools
_contest,

That which is 'best administered is best.

• Turs is a useful old platitude, which, with
some truth, carries in it a• tolerably large
admixture of falsehood. The best, as well as
the 'worst, form of government may be well
or ill-administered, and, as it is admitted that
to make a silk purse out of a sow's ear is a
difficult job, so we presume, that in govern-
ment a good structure may be much more
easily and satisfactorily worked than a bad
one. Nevertheless, it would be folly not to
admit that our best ideal forms, when reduced
to practice, disappoint our hopes, occasionally
through their own inherent vices of structure,
and sometimes in consequence of the dishonest
and evil method of their working. The perfect
Republics of PLATO, Mont, BERKLEY, and
others, are very pleasant to read about; but
the practical travestie called a Republic in the
hands of M. TfIIERS is a very ugly thing to
contemplate. There are explanations, no doubt,
but people get tired of explanations when they
want facts; and forms, however excellent,
become unsatisfactory when the spirit falls.
In America there is a magnificent experi-
ment going on, which we do not for a moment
doubt will finally seitle this much disputed
question. At present the scramble for wealth
interferes with and impedes the struggle for
justice, and the greeq of money over-rides and
dominates the rights of labour. Time and an
increased culture will right this; whilst the
gradual diminishing of the terrible, ignorant,
half-savage surplus, which Europe has for Belong
a time been casting out on the shores of the
great Western Republic, will leave that won-
derful nation more free to develope itself in ac-
cordance with its beneficent ideal, and to grow
abundantly rich by the labour of that surplus
of human creatures which has always been to
Europe an affliction and a reproach. In the
meantime there are many things in con-
nection with the American Republic which
every honest man must condemn whatever
his political opinions. But when we turn
from America to France, we can feel nothing
but shame at the utter lack of principle; the
want of thought for the nation and its welfare;
the manner in which a great people have fallen
off into factions, eaeh contending for some
poor, personal, or sectional interest, utterly
contemptible and mean, in the presence of a
nation perishing for lack of thought and
noble impulse.
In France, what is visible in America, and
apparent enough here—namely, jealousy of
labour; fear of plander on the part of the rich
by the poor; frantic apprehension, lest those
who work should rob and ruin those who pos-
sess, seems to have taken possession of all the
middle and upper classes as a master thought.
Hence those Imperial policies, with middle
class approval, which drove thoughtful men
mad. Hence the wild protest of the Commune
against the corrupt and disgraceful acts of the
governing classes; and hence, whets Paris
was taken, those horrible slaughters, the his-
tory of whichthe commonest feelings of human-
ity makes us anxious to discredit. And hence,
too, the hunting down of the' miners in the
Pas de Calais going on at the present moment.
When we read that the miners have gone to
work again in Denain and Anzin, but that the
strike continues at Aniche, Marie, Ferray,
and in the neighbourhood of Douai, With the
accompaning
,information that the rioters—
that is the
_risen on strike—have in several
places been pursued by cavalry, we know
pretty well bow the affair stands, and we
know also what must be the great, the all-
important battle; the working men of the

A Republic in France, pursuing working
men with e. cavalry, which could not defend
the sacredness of its soil ; a Republic hunting
down dissatisfied workers; Bashing its sabres
in the faces of poor men demanding higher
wages; set in motion by a Republican chief,
the safety of whose position is in the hands of.
one of the most corrupt and mercenary middle
classes in the world, is not a spectacle for
liberal men to admire, especia' ly with those
occasional grim interludes at Satory which
almost hint an alliance, offensive rather than
defensive,. between Versailles and Pande-
monium. We do not blame the French
Republic for this abominable state of things.
Matters are not muoh better in the district
of the Borinage, Belgium, where " Sire"
LEOPOLD reigns. The same battle has to be
fought under all forms of government, and until
it has been won—until labour has emancipated
itself—all else will be little more than bye-
play, important, no doubt, fairly and aotively
to be contended for; but never to be put before
or exalted above the grand battle for the
emancipation of industry which the trades
unions and the co-operative idea propagated
and perfected in practice, must work out as a
necessary preliminary to the success of per-
manent political emancipation..

NEEDLE WOMEN.
The " Song of the Shirt' has gone out of
fashion, and the needlewomen, notwitnstand-
ing cheap bread and all the other wonderful, ,
ameliorations of the age, are still stitching
their own shrouds along with other garments •
as part of their daily work. The Pall-Mall
Gazette gives a ghastly account of the poor
sewers of shrouda in Liverpool. One
woman, a mantle maker, works twelve hours -
a day, at from five to twelve shillings per
week. This is the best case given. A young
woman, a plain sewer, worked eleven hours
a day and received a weekly salary of
seven shillings. An old woman who had been
many years at plain sewing, worked five days
for one shilling and sixpence. A middle-
aged woman, who worked at sack-making
from half-past seven in the morning till six in
the evening, with half an hour for dinner, got
4s. per week. A young woman said she was
machinist, and made youths' single jackets,
for which she was paid at the rate of fivepenoe
for four. It took her half a day to make
the four. When she came out at night, she ,
added, after working a heavy maohine all
day, she could hardly stand on her feet.
Another machinist, who' made gentlemen's '-
trousers at 3s. per dozen, and for the very best
45., if she worked from six in the morning
to twelve at night, could with the assistance
of a taster, make half a dozen, out of which
she had to find her own thread and silk.
Another woman got, for making linen cuffs
and collars, lid. per dozen, and earned od. a
day by working from nine to seven o'clock.
But why go further over this horrible bead-
roll of misery? There is enough here, in all
conscience, to show us what a dreadful life of
agony some of our women-workers pass; and

Perhaps so; but it would, nevertheless, ho
