THE FOOD AND WAGES QUESTION.

TII E time is very near when the trades

anions that are doing their best to procure
better wages for labour will receive a strong
impetus from the cries of distress which the
dearness of living is beginning to extort from
all who are dependent upon fixed incomes and
personal earnings. In this way thousands of
middle-class people, who had talked rather big
about the dissatisfaction of the working
classes, will learn, it may be hoped, to sym-
pathise with them. At any rate, the tendency
of things is, to convince all except those whom
nothing can either convince or persuade, that
the rate of wages must not merely have respect
to the value of the work done, but must also
take into consideration the price of the neoes-
series of life.

By almost the smallest majority possible,
the carpenters' and joiners' delegation have
decided to accept, as a compromise, fifty-one
hours, at eightpence-halfpenny an hour, till
March 1, 1873, instead of standing out longer
for the nine hours' day at ninepence an hour.
When, in a body of more than six-score men,
the majority who carried the point was but
three, it is easy to understand the real feelin g
of the trade. There comes a time when half a
loaf is held better than no bread.

i The conviction of a single railway porter
under the " Molestation " Act, need not be

anxiously considered, anyway. Supposing
the man to have his own want of self-control
to thank for the month's imprisonment to

which he has been sentenced by Mr. HANNAY,
all we ask) those of the general public who

watch such things to take note of, is the fact
that COOKE, does not belong to any regular
trade or handicraft, but to a promiscuous
body of men who, generally Speaking, would
not, perhaps, be found accepting that position
had they been brought up to any regular and
fixed occupation involving special knowledge
and skill, and affording the prospect of good
wages. The most important fact that has
transpired in connection with this affair, is
the statement of the SECRETint of the London
and South-Western Railway. Company, that
the Directors have conceded to the clerks and
men tin increase of wages in answer to their
memorial. We shall see what may follow at
Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, and other
plices. In the meantime, the men in the
service of Cnantri and lionir E, and of another
large firm of carriers, have done as much
service to those who think themselves unjustly
treated by honourably acknowledging the
fair conduct of their own employers to them-
selves, as they could have done, by any form
of more direct and palpable sympathy. Every
instancein which employers and employed have
arrived at a good mutual understanding
without severe pressure on either side, is a
service done to the cause of labour and
industry at large.
The Police Committee of the City of London
have secured from the Common Council an
increase of pay in answer to the memorial of
the constables to the Commissioners. Third-
class constables are to have 245. a week
instead of 215.; second-class 275. instead of
245. 6d.; and first-class 30s. instead of 28s.
Second-class serjeants are to have 345. instead
of 315.; first-class 375. instead of 345.; and so
on through the other grades, the whole
increase amounting to £5,000. This is a
palpable recognition, on the highest practical

-authority in the kingdom, of the unanswer-
able claim to a universal advance of wages in
order to enable those who are dependent upon
them to subsist at the present rate of food and
other prices. The discussions going on re-
specting the superannuation allowances to the
police, and which interest the whole body
throughout the whole country, will have an
excellent tendenoy to promote the consoli-
dation of all trade interests of every kind.

articles.text:
PRIESTS AND GOVERNMENTS.

THE POPE and the CannuaLs have not
taken long to convince themselves that their
policy of participating in the municipal
elections of the Italian kingdom was not quite
so astute as that of priests is supposed usually
to be. AU the elections which took place on
Sunday last, we are told, was favourable to
the Liberals; and iu all the cities and
towns, there were triumphal flags, baud' of

music, and general rejoicing., Had the priests
abstained,. their nudisplayed strength might
have preserved its reputation for vastness;
but, having been Put forth without success, it
has demonstrated its perfect weakness. Their
resolution to interfere had the positive effect
of healing all the breaches which dispute and
rivalry had made among the Liberals. Of
course, . the defeated faction fall back upon
such cries as that of persecution. As though
they would have accepted the constitution or
the kingdom, notwithstanding the seven
dozen other , articles, had the first, which
declares the Church of Rome to be the religion
of the State, been kept to 'their mind; they
make the air ring with their hypocritical wail.
"How can you expect us to keep to the Con-
stitution, when, you begin yourselves with
violating its first principle ?" The answer is
easy, obvious, and conclusive; 'when the Con-
stitution was made, the POPE had not issued
his "Syllabus," nor had proclamation been
made of the monstrous dogma of his HOLINESS'S
infallibility.- Might not a lesson be drawn by
ourselves from the Italian instance, with
reference to the best manner of treating in-
termeddling priests. As the lunatic said to
the officer who answered that he carried, a
sword to "kill his enemies to be sure," so
•we might say of these priests, "They'll die of
themselves, if you let them alone ;" whereas,
if we make martyrs of them by legal prosecu-
tion, we may not merely prolong their days,
but even revive their energies.

PROGRESS OF AFFAIRS IN FRANCE.
PaosrEcrrs brighten of the establishment of
the ‘i Conservative Republic" • in France.
The FREsID ENT has the satisfaction of seeing
the great loan taken up with unparalleled
rapidity and. confidence. The amount of sub-
scriptions is More than fourteen times the
sum required. ' The departments of France
have contributed about
,a third as much as
the capital; and nearly half of the whole has
come from the different money markets of
Europe, London taking the lead, and. Frank-
fort and.. Cologne following, Bombay even
furnishing nearly a million sterling. The
FINANCE MINISTER, transported bejond that
coldness of blood which usually characterizes
Such persons, regards the event asi a decibiyo
mark of patriotic and general confidence in
the Government of M. Trtmus, and speaks in
a One of pions acknowledgment of Divine
PROVIDENCE thiit isnot often, illd tlike4 by French
statesmen. It is noteworthy, moreover, that
this strain of sentiment elicited cheers from
the Republican portion of the Assembly, while
the supporters of Church and Thione were in
no humour for thanksgivalg.
M. GAIIIIETTA. is gathering fresh moral
strength against the favourable conjuncture, in
which, perchance, a vigorous young man may
leap into the saddle now occupied by a man of
firm nerve but of great age. As far as he is
himself concerned, the head of the Administra-
tion, during the war, at Bordeaux, is content
to repeat, that he will be judged by a fair
comparison between the resources of the
country as they stood when he took office and
as they where when he resigned and now were.
Perhaps the best defence that M. NAQITET, who
arranged the contracts of which the Right
assailed themselves as ground of accusation,
could make for himself, or get made for him,
would have been to confess that he was better
at chemistry than in artillery, though no proof
is apparent that he took money for getting M.
GAMB ETTA'S signatures to suspicions contracts.
Even Duke PasQuan, 'before finishing his
irritating speech, was fain,. not simply to
exculpate M. GAMBETTIL altogether, but even
to intimate that the Commission of Inquiry in
which he presiaed had no wish for the
Assembly to endorse the blame whiph they
had thrown upon M. NAQIJET. If all this was
meant to save the Right from the thrusts, the
cuts, and the blows of M. GAMBETTA'S
eloquence, it wholly failed of its design. The
members of the Right appeared to feel, that the
mischief which they prepared for the orator and
his party, had recoiled upon their own heads;
and the opinion of dispassionate observers
is, that they have lost and he has gained by
this last encounter, not improbably the very
last before the parliamentary recess..
Had. Anything . been wanting to make the

course pursued by M. TEETERS intelligible and
clear, it has been supplied by what he said in
the Committee of Prorogation. The Republic,
he said, was entrusted to him, and he con-
sidered it his duty to preserve that deposit
intact, He would do all he could to make it
a Conservative Republic, having a deep horror
of anarchy. By governing "correctly," he
would maintain the pact of Bordeaux. While
he would discountenance unlawful manmuvres
for the dissolution of the Assembly during the
vacation (from to-morrow to November 15th),
he would nut attempt to binder peaceful ngi •
tation, for that purpose. His own views of
government were in harmony with the Eng.
Rah Constitution; but, as there were no fewer
than three families claiming the throne, he
should devote his efforts to the consolidation of
the Conservative Republic
.as the best for
France, if not the only form possible under
the circumstances. •

articles.title: NEW AGITATION.
articles.text:
A NEW AGITATION.

It will be seen from another column, that the
working men who touk part in Mr. Samuel
Morley's political reunion at the Cannon-street
hotel, :have published the platform which was
adopted as the result of three night's deliberation.
It classifies the reforms yet to be achieved under
three heads—political, social, and financial. In
the first, a prominent place is assigned to the
assimilation of borough and county voting, to pay-
ment of members, proportional representation,
and shorter Parliaments. Among the social
desiderata are the total abolition of the game laws,
purchase of the railways by the State, acquisition
by the State of cultivable waste and other lands,
disestablishment of State Churches, and the
creation of county boards analogous to the Metro-
politan Board of Works. Foremost in what is
required of Mr. Lowe stands a thorough revision
of the Civil List. To that are subordinated direct
fixiition, military retrenchment, readjustment of
the income tax, and equitable rating for local
fixation. The authors of this comprehensive
platform pronounce the "old Liberal programme"
to be "well-nigh amaitusted."

That this meeting regrets the tone of the de-

THE DIFFICULTIES OF THE COTTON

TRADE.

Mr. Hugh Mason, President of the Manchester
Chamber of Commerce, at a quarterly meeting
held on Wednesday, in reviewing the subjects
which had been under the consideration of the
directors during the last quarter, said the duties
of the directors during that period bad been of a
multifarious an 3 very important character. They
had considered the questions and the hours of
labour in factories, of railway amalgamation, the
Mersey Railway Bill, the Dill of Entry, the
Anglo-French Treaty, the question of the native
Princes of India, the Public Health Dill, the
County Court and Bankruptoy business, the Nine
Hours Bill, Fiji cotton, the adulteration of Ame-
rican cotton, the Embassy from Japan, and the
wipe tariffs of Spain and Portugal. The Chamber
met that day, he was very sorry to say, under very
unfavourable circumstances with regard to the great
trade of this county. What with the advance in
the price of coal and of other materials connected
with our machine making and manufacturing
establishments, the advance in the wages of the
workpeople, and the unsettledness in the conduct
of the workpeople generally, the condition of those
who had invested their capital was one of intense
anxiety and perplexity. 110 himself did not cast
by any means the whole of the blame in COllllOO.

tier' with the profitless state of the cotton trade
upon the working pi ople. He believed that no
small amount of the blame rested upon those who
had invested their capital in that business, and
who at one time showed an irrational over-confi.
deuce, and at another betrayed a senseless panic.
Three were very much to blame for the preeent
profitless and fluctuating state of the trade.
did not overlook the fact either, that the labour
market of this country had been drained to ail
unusual extent by etnigrat'on, 196,000 men and
women, besides children, having left our shores rj
1871, a not insignificant portion of whom hal left
the county of Lancaster. That, in connection
with other unfaVourable circumstances, bad mill.
tated very much indeed against the prosperity of
the cotton trade. In addition, there was the high
price of the raw material. The cotton trade had
never been prosperous with the raw material at a
high price. Looking forward to the next six
months, he thought every gentleman engaged in
the trade would agree with him that they had
before them a very fluctuat:ng, uncertain, and
anxious state of things. It behoved the trade for
the next six months to be exceedingly cautious.
The meeting was also addressed by Mr. C. Thornpg,
son, Mr. Alderman Bennett, Mr. R. Johnson, vice!
president, and other gentlemen, and the proceed,
logs terminated.

ANTI-GAME LAW CONFERENCE.

A conference to consider the advisability of
estalalishing an Anti. Game Law League was
held on Wednesday evening at the West-
minster Palace Hotel; Mr. Weston in the
chair. The attendance was very small, although
a mach larger number of working men than
the whole audience amounted to had signed a
circular urging the total abolition of the game
laws. The chairman urged that the working
classes were, and had long been, unanimous
on this question, and held that the
game laws were inicluituus and ought to he
abolished; hut they had no confidence what-
ever in the Special Committee of the House of
Commons which was chosen to deal with the
subject. He also explained that the meeting
was the following up of a: resolution arrived at
some time ago by the Land and Labour
League, to which ha belonged. Mr. I', A.
Taylor, M.P., described the present position Of
the question in Parliament. He said it was nO
longer a question in the country whether the
game laws were or were not bad; all parties
had long ago agreed that they were unendur-
able. Under the present laws Scotland was a
vast sporting field, lie pointed out that had
farming was one of the results of the game
Jaws, that the labouring classes therefore
suffered from them, that the prosecutions in-
stituted under the game laws had a most
demoralising effect, and that the House or
Commons as a tribunal to settle the questiou
was utterly incompetent, the Government, in
fact, having 'acted in as miserable and con-
temptible a manner with respect to the game
laws as in 'some other matters.

Mr. Holyoake moved, and Ur. Galbraith
seconded, the following resolution
That the privilege conferred by the State upon
the landed aristocracy by the enactment of the
game laws, which have caused such ino,rleulable
evils, is one that ought no longer to be tolerated,
and in consequence of the apathy of the present
House of Commons, this meeting. resolves itself
into an Anti-Game Law League, and pledges itself
to use its utmost endeavours to seoure the total
abolition of those obnoxious laws.
_

A discussion ensued, but it was understood
that the proceedinks should be more conversa-
tional than an opportunity for the delivery of
set speeches. The resolutiont after debates
was carried unanimously, and a committee
was formed and preliminary steps taken for
the formation of a League iu accordance with
the resolution,

A gentleman from Boothuid, at the close of
meeting, said he had no doubt the . League
would receive more support in his. country
than in England, fOr deer arid grouse were the
Highlander's greatest enemies, and he had no
hesitation in saying that within five years of
the abolition of the game laws in It cotland
the agricultural productions there would be
doubled.

A vote of thanks to Mr. P. A. Taylor, M.P.,
and the chairman, closed the proceedings.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

On Monday, in the House of Lords, Lord
Derby called attention to the correspondence
which bad taken place between Mr. Ayrton
and Dr. Hooker respecting the changes lately
made at Kew Garden' s condemning the course
adopted by the Lords of the Treasury, and
asking for an explanation of the conduct of the
First Commissioner of Works. The Duke of
St. Albans defended the Beard of Works from
the charge of wishing to get rid of Dr.
Hooker, and Lord Halifax followed with
the intention of explaining Mr. yrton's,
doings.

It was stated by the City Remembraneer,
at a meeting of the Common Council, that the
Government had complied with the request to
Insert the name of the Corporation in the
Public Ilealth Bill, as the sanitary authority
for the River Thames ; and, after some dis-
'mission as to the extent of the powers thus
conferred, the carrying out of the measure
was placed in the hands of a committee.

An increase of pay to the City Police Force,
amounting in all to more than £5,000 a year,
was unanimously approved .by the Court of
Common Council. It will be remethbered that
the men exhibited lately some dissatisfaction
with the existing rates, but that they were
promptly and judiciously met half-way by the
authorities.

At Saturday's sitting of the House of Com-
mons, Mi. Bruce carried the Licensing Bill
half-way over the difficulty of the 24th clause.
His proposal to grant a certain amount of
discretion to provincial magistrates in respect
of the hours of closing, was favourably enter-
tained by Sir Robert Anstrather and other
licensing reformers. Having promised to pre-
pare an amendment in this sense by Tuesday
night, ho proceeded with that part of the
'clause referring to the metropolis. On an
amendment of Mr. Looke's that the hours of
closing on Sunday be from three to five in-
stead of from three to six, the committee
divided, giving a majority of eighty-four for
the longer term. The openirig hour on week
days was fixed at five o'clock.

Mr. W. °swell Livingstone writes that the
painful reflections which have been made on
Dr. Kirk are the result of a misconception on
the part of his father, which, while he was at
Zanzibar, he endeavouted in his letters to
remove. He declares that "Dr. Kirk is
to-
tally undeserving of the accusations which
arc daily reaching the public."

Mdllo. Nilsson has become Madame Rou-
zaud. The wedding service attracted such a
crowd to Westminster Abbey that, after
eleven o'clock, admission had to be refused.
At the wedding breakfast, which was served
at the house of Mr. Cavendish Bentinek,
M.P., there was a splendid assnniblage of
Celebrities, fashionable, diplomatic, and mu-
sical. The preiients, which have been valued
at .R 12,000 included a magnificent gold
bracelet from the Princess of Wales.

the remains of the Duke of Guise were on
Saturday- committed to the family vault at
Dreux, the funeral service being attended by
many prominent members of the Right, and by
foregn notabilities, including General Sher-
man.

King Amadeus has been saluted at Valla-
dolid by a ery of " Viva La Republique! "
only one however, and from a Frenchman,
who was'foithwith arrested.

Rome will witness Shortly a meeting of the
Jesuit chiefs. It has been convoked by Father
Beck, general of the Order.

The latest explorer of Nicaragua, Mr. Cross-
man, reports in favour of the practicability of
of an Inter-oceanic, ship canal,

In reply to the Earl Of Shaftesbury's
memorial respeeting the A.thanasian Creed,
the two Primates have minutely reviewed all
past proceedings and proposals for the modifi-
cation of the damnatory clauses. While
promising their aid in furthering the wishes
of the memorialists, they express a belief that
legitimate scruples on the ether side can also
be respected.
-

France "passed through a grand crisis of
financial patriotism on the first day of sub-
scription to the Three Milliard Loan. The
crowd which intended to lodge its deposits at
the Palais de Plndustrie bivouacked all night
on the Elysian Fields, and formed itself
en queue before sunrise. Bankers and ex-
change agents of all kinds throughout the city
received subscriptions without commission.
At night a Paris Correspondent learned from
M. Goulard that three times the amount of
issue had. been subscribed, and that foreign
capitalists bad invested far more freely than
they did in last year's loan. The premium
already stands at 3 to 4 per cent, on private
oleo. *

Miss Jex Blake and the female medical
students have scored another victory in the
Court of Session. Lord Gifford has affirmed
their right to be ednop.ted and to graduate at
the University on the same footing as male
students.

Three prosecutions before the Greenwich
Police-Court in respect of children detained
from school ended in the infliction of con-
ditional fines of li. each. 'One defendant
pleaded that he and his wife left home at six
o'clock in the morning, and the girl who onght
to be at school was their only housekeeper.
Another of them had seven children, three of
them under four years of age. But the Bench
seems to have accepted that confession in a
very Malthusian spirit; it did not reckon in
mitigation of damages.

From Madrid we learn that a Carlist band
recently succeeded in carrying off 13 men
employed on the Saragossa and Barcelona.
Railway Company, for whose reason they de-
manded a large sum of money. Later ad vices
state that the band, which consisted of 1,000
men, has been dispersed by the troops with the
loss of 13 killed, and 35 prisoners, 10 of the
latter being wounded. Another Carlist band
has been defeated, with a loss of three killed
and several wounded.

The French Assembly has passed the final
clauses of the Tariff Bill. The Parliamentary
struggle against the taxation of raw materials
is now, therefore, at an end.

At Versailles, on Saturday, the principal
topic of conversation among the members of
the French Assembly was the energetic letter
of M. Thiers to the Prefect or the Pas-
de-Calais, in which department some of the
late mining didturbances have occurred, de-
claring that the Government would repress all
disorders with a firm hand.

It is stated in a Paris telegram that in con.
sequenee of the death of Juarez, the French
Government is about to re-establish diplomatic
relations with Mexico.

A large number of the inhabitants of the
east of London on Sunday assembled near the
Betbnal-green Museum to pass resolutions in
favour of opening that institution to the work-
ing classes on Sundays. Owing, however, to
the interference of the police, nothing was
done.

The Local Government Board have declined
to accede to the suggestion that the Small-pox
Hospital at Hampstead should be used for the
reception of harmless persons of the chronic
or imbecile class. It is held that it would not
be expedient to divert tho institution from the
purpose for which it was originally designed,
"and which it has so admirably fulfilled."

The Irish "National" papers profess to
regard with satisfaction the resolve of the
Government to prosecute the Bishop of Clon-
fert, Captain Nolan, Mr. Sebastian Nolan,
and nineteen priests, on a charge of intimida-
tion. The ground of their approval is that
the proceedings .will be the means of for over
destroying the confidence of the Irish people
in Whig administrations.

Vice-Chancellor Bacon had before him on
Saturday an information filed at the instance
of certain inhabitants at Gravelly-hill, near
Birmingham, to restrain the Town Council of
that borough from committing a nuisance by
carrying on sewage works at Saltley. An
injunction had already been granted, and a,
motion was now made for an order of sequestra-
tion against the Connell for disobedience of
the injunction. ,The order was granted, but it
is not to be enforced until a specified day in
Michaelmas Term.

At the Wesleyan Conference on Monday
the position of the various chapels with re.
sped to the reduction of the trust debts and
the erection and enlargement of buildings were
the subjects principally dealt with.

The Eloho Challenge Shield and the Snider
and the Irish International Trophies were on
Saturday taken in state to Guildhall upon two
gun carriages belonging to the Hon. Artillery
Company, and escorted by detacmhents from
eleven metropolitan corps. The Eleho Shield
was carried by the English eight who had won
it, headed by Mr. Wells, M.P., their captain,
while the Snider Trophy was borne by Captain
Field of the. English twenty. Each of these
gentlemen made a few observations, which
were responded to by the Lord Mayor.

The education of Wesleyan ministers formed
the subject of discussion at a meeting of the
Theological Institution Committee of the Con-
ference On Saturday. Dr. Rigg, principal of
the Westminster Training College, expressed
his opinion that taking the breadth of the
country, the Methodist pupils would well bear
comparison with those ef other denominations,
fie did not think that any advantage would
be gained by ondeavourmg to conform the
Virealeyan style. of preaching to the etaudard of
"diesentin respectnbility," .

Soldano and Sitbon, the murderers of the
Tunisian merchant Greco, were executed at
Marseilles on Monday morning. It will be
remembered. that Sitbon was captured in
England, and sent back to France under the
Extradition Treaty.

Cholera is said to have reached Berlin, but
the cases reported are not believed to be of the
real Asiatic type.

Dr. Kirk has sent a brief official report con-
cerning Dr. Livingstone to the Bombay
Government. Dr. Kirk says that nothing
whatever is known at Zanzibar of the results
of Dr. Livingstone's travels, or how he intends
to employ the next two years. In his official
correspondence with Zanzibar no mention
whatever is made of his travels.

Both at 'Versailles and in the provinces the
Republicans are declaring themselves more
openly than ever. In the Assembly a motion
has been tabled which would limit the exist-
ence of the present Chamber to February,,
187:3. It..proposes that a general electron be
held then, with a view to introducing a defini-
tive form of Government. At Lyons there has
been a vigorous Movement made to secure a
Republican Prefect in the room of M. Pascal,
promoted to a .Councillorsjiip .of State. M.
Lefrano has readily promised to respect the
wishes of the majority.

A correspondent in Rome says that the
news of the determination of the Government
to prosecute the Irish priests concerned in the
Galway election. proceedings has produced a
profound sensation at the Vatican. The cor-
respondent also calls attention to the fact that
the clerical party has been defeated in the
elections throughout Italy, in which, by a re-
cent change of polioy, it decided to take part.
All the elections which have hitherto come off,
he adds, have resulted in splendid victories for
the Liberals.

The death is announced of Sir James
O'Connell, the youngest and only surviving
brother of the late Daniel O'Connell. The
deceased baronet, who received his title in
1869, expired at his residence Lake View,
near Killarney, at the age of Bd. He is suc-
ceeded by his eldest son, Maurice, born in
1822.

The annual distribution of prizes to the
pupils of the North London Collegiate and
Camden Schools for Girls was made at Willis's
Rooms on Monday by the Bishop of London,
who took occasion to make some pointed
observations on the importance of the educa-
tion of women.

A curious confession of murder was made
by a young woman 'named Ellen King, at
Woolwich, on Tuesday. Going to the police
inspector of that district she stated that she
was walking in Richmond Park with her
sweetheart, when he attempted to take im-
proper liberties with her. She resisted, and
pushed him into the water, when she, without
making any effort to save him, sew him rise
and sink three times. She has been brought
before the Woolwich magistrates and re-
manded, in order that inquiry may be made.

• The Lords Justices have delivered judgment
in the case of Beattie v. Lord Ebury and
others, which was an appeal by his lordship
and other directors of the Watford and
Rickmansworth Railway Company from a
decision of Vice-Chancellor Bacon, whereby
he held that the directors were pefrsonally
liable for a sum of about £22,000, a debt due
from the Watford and Rickmansworth Rail-
way Company to the Union Bank of London
for having overdrawn their account. The
claim made by the Union Bank personally was
founded upon an alleged misrepresentation of
facts by the directors. Their lordships held
that the acts of these gentlemen did not
amount to such a misrepresentation as would
render them personally liable, and allowed the
appeal.

To induce the Lorl Mayor to lend his aid
towards raising a fund in support of Mrs.
Gladstone's Convalescent Home, an influential
deputation waited upon his lordship at the
Mansion House, and, having explained that
the Home was free to all, and that it was
greatly in want of funds, the Lord Mayor
promised to open a list of subscriptions and to
hold a meeting early in October for the par.
poses suggested by the deputation.

Mr. It. It, Torrens, ALP., has been ap-
pointed a Knight Commander of the Order of
St. Michael stud St. George, in recognition of
colonial services, and more especially in con-
nection with the Registration of Titlei to
Land Act, first enacted in South Australia,
and subsequently adopted by other Australian
colonies.

The Due d'Aumale is represented as having
said eo certain of his friends after the (Lath
of his son, "I have no more happineis to
expect; no ambition to satisfy. But let it be
known I will not fail to fulfil my duty towards
my couutry."

Dr Aldis, the well-known officer of health
of St. George's, Hanover-square, is dead.

Another fatal railway accident, resulting
from the dilatory shunting of a goods train.,
in front of an approaching passenger train,
took place on Monday, the collision occurring
about two miles from Hereford. A carriage,
in which were several persons, was smashed to
pieces; a boy was killed and several people
were seriously injured. A great destruction,
of rolling stock is reported; and many pas-
sengers otherwise unhurt have been severely
shaken.

Ira Ma-dozen street Arabs were charged
before Mr. Benson at Southwark Police
-
court with sleeping in vans and under arch-
ways—the prosecutor being one of the London
School Board's officers. The urchins, of most,
of whom a very bad account was given, were
sent to various industrial schools and training
ships.

Forty-one and a half milliards of francs
£1,660,000,000 sterling—such is the tre-
mendous total of the subscriptions to the
great French loan announced by M. Goulard
in the Assembly on Tuesday; and it would
appear that even yet the marvellous tale is not,
complete, for the returns have not fully come
in. Judging from the tenor of some of the
earlier accounts, the subscription's would seem
to have been equally divided between France
and foreign countries; the Departments, how-
ever, figuring for so comparatively, triiling.a
sum as to suggest some unexpected failure in
the patriotism or the resources of the, rural
population. The contribution of England to
the most incredible total is believed to be
about six milliards. ,On the Bourse on Tues-
day the loan closed it 88f. 40c.---nearly 31.
above the issue price.

Senator Sumner has addresso I a letter to
the coloured citizens of the Milted States,
declaring himself strongly in favour of Mr.
Horace Greeley for the Presidency.

Continuing his progress from Santander,
the King of Spain has been nost warmly re-
ceived by the population. His Majesty vill
now return to Madrid.

The Queen of. the Belgians has been safely
delivered of a daughter.

During a firelit "Uxbridge 'a peculiarly cou-
rageous act was performed. A large oil and
colourshop was in a blaze,and when the fire-
engine had arrived it was discovered that no
water was in the reservoir which supplied the,
town. It was, however, found that next door.
to the burning building were several barrels
of gunpowder ; and as the flames were spread-'
ing, and no time was to be lost, a number of
men volunteered to fetch out the explosive
material. This they accomplished amidst
showers of sparks, and, fortunately, without
any accident oocurring.

There was a review of the Norwich and
Norfolk Volunteers on Wednesday in ICetter-
inghani-park, the seat of Sir T. Boileau, A
party of the 7th Dragoon Guards took part in
the manceuvres.

The godfather of the newly-born Belgian
Princess is to be the Prince of Wales, and her
godm3ther the Duchess Clementine of kiiixe-
Cobur,g.

The petroleum depots at Hunter's Point,
opposite New York, have been burned. Thu
loss is estimated at 1,000,000 dollars., The
depas mostly oontaiued oil.

The Great Eastern Railway Company is
importing Belgian coal rid Harwich.

The Liberals will, it is stated, contest North
Derbyshire at the next election, bringing
forward Lord George Cavendish and another.

The following Minute has been drawn UP
by the Committee of .Council ou Education
with respect ta schools used as polling .places
—Read—Section 6 of the Ballot Act, 1872,
and Article 19 of the New Code, 1872. ite-
solyed—That if a school is etnoloyed for the
purpose of taking the poll at a Parliamentary
election, under section 6 of the Ballot Act,
1872, the number of meetings during wiljuh
the managers are deprived of the use of the
school solely in consequence of its being k°
employed,, may, if necessary, be counted
under Article 19.01 the New 'Code in making
up-1. The 400 meetings of the school re",
quire& by that lirtiole ; or, 2. The 250 at-
tendances of any sc!iolar who was untle!
instruotion in the school the week before a
was occupied for election purposes.

An inorease of py .tothe City porco'foreet
amountivg to upwards of £5,000 a year, Ava
agreed upon at a meeting of the Counacei
Council.

At the Mansion House on Saturday, Franic
Miner, 35 years of age, was charged with the'
murder of IL.vbert Salt, by etibbingltiiu. #
re wid for a week wag granted.

AUG. 3, 1872.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday
considerable amusement was created by a
motion made by Mr. C. Forster that the peti-
tion from the inhabitants of Manchester against
the Licensing Bill should be rejected. It was
stated that the names of Mr. Gladstone, Alr.
Lowe, IS4r. Bright, and Sir Wilfrid Lawson
were all appended to the petition, and that
altogether 178 fictitious signatures had
already been discovered. The motion having
been agreed to, Mr. Graves proposed an in-
quiry into the present means of manning
the navy, and advocated the education of
seamen of the mercantile marine by the
State.

At Osborne on Tuesday, Lord Lyveden
received from the Queen the insir.,rna of the
Knighthood of the, Bath; and Mr. George
Bidden Airy and Mr. Arthur Helps the
insignia of Knights-Commanders of the
Order.

Paris journals publish a telegram from her
llajesty the Queen condoling with the Due
d'Aumale on the recent death of his son, the
Dtic de guise. I s a wife who has lost her
husband, and a mother lately in dread of
losing her son, the Queen feels herself pecu-
liarly able to sympathise with the bereaved
father.

his Royal Highness Prince Arthur distri-
butrd the prizes to the successful scholars at
Dover College on Tuesday.

It is said that the new Board of Education
in Scotland is to meet for the first time in the
third week of October next, and is to it
thereafter regularly throughout the year, with
the exception of the mouths of Augubt and
September,

It is said that Madame Milnre, widow of
the. Socialist writer.who was shot without any
trial' during.the last days of the Commune,
op the steps of the Pantlnlort, is about to bring
an action for damages against Captain Garcia,
the stuff officer who ordered her husband to be
executed,

The announcement of Sir Richard Wallaee
having become proprietor of the late Lord
Hertford's estates, in County Antrim, has been
received by the tenantry with great demon-
strations of joy. Mutires blazed on the hills,
tar barrels wore burned in the square of:
Lisburn, and the inhabitants cxhibikd the
utmost enthusiasm.

The Queen and suite will arrive in Edin-
burgh on the 14th August, and start for Bal-
moral on the evening of the 16th.

The Governor-General of India has written
to the Earl of Shaftesbury as follows:
" Ple(,s3 attach my name, if it is n)t too hle,
to the Declaration about the Athanasian
Creed. I entirely agreed with it, and think
it now Trite time for the laity to make them-
selves heard."

It is authoritatively stated that the diary
of Dr. Livingstone, forwarded to Miss Living-
stone will .in no case be published unless
intelligence of the great explorer's death
reaches England. The diary was, scaled by
the Doctor himself, with instructions to this
effect.

To prepare for the annual meeting of the
National Artillery Association, which com-
mences on 'Monday next,
.180 men of the
Sheffield Artillery Volunteers, under Colonel
Creswick, have left their work at the busiest
time, and sacrificed a week's wages, to per-
form at Shoeburyness duties which hitherto
have fallen to the Royal Artillery. With
comparatively poor inducements in the shape
of prizes, the desire to attend the meeting is
so great on the part of the Artillery Volun-
teers that many detachments have this year
again been refused en account of the limited
accommodation for the meeting at the School
of Gunnery.

Before the Judicial Committee of the Privy
Council, it was stated, in reference to the
suit brought by General Forrester against the
Secretary of State for India to recover certain
arms and military stores seized by the Indian
Government in 1836, with 12 per cent.
interest from that date—that the parties,bad
been unable to accept their lorditip's sug-
gestion, and agree to an amount or an arbitra-
tion. The appellant was quite willing to
accept the Lord Chancellor's proposal that the
question should now be left to the Committee;
but on the other side this was declined. Ul-
timately their lordships undertook to inquire
into the matter.

Lord William Hay's appeal against a decree
of the Chief Court of the Punjaub, which
-pronounced that his lordship had committed
adultery with Mrs. Gordon, was further beard
before the Judicial Committee, and was
allowed ; with costs for the appellant, both in
India and in this country.

During an adjourned inquiry before the
coroner at Camberwell into the circumstances
connected with the death of a child named
Hoxley, in a lodging-house, it was stated that
the infant vas •scarcely ever fed, and that the
mother was often heard to say she wished the
child was dead. Some revolting particulars
were given respecting the state in which the
lodgers at the house lived and slept; and the
Rev. Mr. Thorpe stated that other children
had been 'educed to a similarly emaciated
condition in the same house. The coroner
decided, however, that this could not be
admitted in evidence; and the inquest was
then adjourned.

A charge of violating the provisions of the
Gun Barrel Proof Act, 1868, by keeping for
exportation a large quantity of unproved
small arms, was preferred at Worship-street
Police-court against Mr. Michael Coleman
Cohen. A number of the guns were old flint-
locks of the time of George 111. It was
alleged that the arms were intended for ex-
portation to the Malays; but the contention
for the defence was that the evidence had
failed, and, as the arms were only delivered on
the afternoon of the 12th, and seized on the
followine, morning, the defendant had no time
to get them proved. The magistrate admitted
that the evidence was weak, and dismissed
the case.

A treaty between Belgium and England for
the extradition of criminals has been signed,
and will come into operation in two months.

Francis De*, the eminent Libcral Hun-
garian, who has been seriously ill, is now
recovering.

We are authorised to _state that the diary
of Dr. Livingstone, forivarded to Iliss .Living-
stone, now in Ireland, will in no case be
published, unless intelligence of the great
explorer's death reaches England; and, that
the diary was sealed by the doctor himself
With instructions to that efreet: The Royal
Geographical Society, probably alive to the
inexpediency of 'prolonging Suspense as to
the conduct of the respective members- of the
relief expedition till the meeting of the British
Association at Brighton, have resolved to
issue to the subscribers of the Search and
Relief Fund printed copies of the letters of
the leaders of the expedition and an account
of their experiences uninediately.—Freenawi's
tToirrnal.

, In anticipation of the appointment of the
Attorney-General for Ireland to a judgeship,
Mr. John Ilea, a well-known solicitor of
Belfast, has issued an address to the electors
of Derry on Orange principles.

On Wednesday the Rev. Luke' H. Wise-
man was. elected President- of the Wesleyan
Conference, having received 356 votes. The:
Rev. G. T. Parks, who was supported by 238
votes,- was chosen Secretary."

With reference to tho similar oaseleard at
Guildhall Police-court, respecting a quantity
of French muskets alleged to have been sold
in England, Messrs. Caspar state that the
barrels had all been duly stamped, marked,
and certified, the only irregularity being that
they had not been rgistered in England.
Two, however, bore the mark of, the London
proof house. Only the lowest penalty was
inflicted on one summons, and no penalty or -
costs on the other two.

At the interview which took place on
Monday between M. niers and the members
of the Prorogation Committee, the former
again declared that as the Republic had been
confided to him, it was hi duty ta maintainit
intact. He was using all his efforts to mak()
it a Conservative Republic. He bad long
been attached to constitutional monarchy as
in England, but in presence of: three rival
dynasties that form of Government did not
seem suitable for France. A COuiervative
Republic alone appeared to him capable of
preserving peace and order.

•
A correspondent at .Versailles says that at
the sitting of the French Assembly on Tuesday
the angry. scenes of the previous day appeared
to be forgotten, and scarcely anything was
talked about by members but the success of
the new Loan. Some of the remarks made by
the Finance Minister in announcing that
success were badly. received bythe night, but
everyone was in suet' good humour that calm-
ness soon returned. According to the Ladd
petulance Beige,: Belgium has, .comparatively
speaking, played the most important part of
any country, in connection with this great
financial operation. The sum she has sub.
scribed, amounts, it says, to more than nine
milliards of francs.

Earl Spencer bas been appointed Lord
Lieutenant of Northamptonshire, vice the late
Lord Southampton.

The Empress of the FreneE, the Prince
Imperial, and suite arrived at Ediiihurgh on
Tuebday evening, and froceeded to the Royal
Ilotel, where they are expected to remain a
few days before going to the Highlands.

The minority of five who voted on Tuesday
night with Mr. Auberon Ileibert in favour of
retaining the Lords' amendment to the pre-
amble of the Scotch Education Bill, consisted
of Mr. Candlish, Mr. Morrison, Mr. IL
Richard, Mr. Stapleton, and Mr. Watkin
Williams.

Sir Edwin Landieer is said to be slowly re-

S/11,—Your leading article of July 13th

late agricultural meeting, in which he refers
at some length to the present aspect of the
agricultural labour question. Your article
blames the bishop for his remarks on what he
calls "outside interference."
Now, sir, in a case of dispute like this, it is
advisable to clear the ground for argument by
ascertaining the facts of the case. One fact is
worth a dozen arguments, and if a man cannot
bring facts to support his argument, his ease
must be a weak one. What, then, are the facts
of the "labour question."l
held in my hand a return of the value of
ordinary agricultural labourer?' ;wages in
various countries, extracted from the Farmers'

135.; Warwickshire, Is.; Worceetershire,
16s; Yorkshire, 18s.
Now it must be remembered tharthese re-
turns do not accurately give the full amount

only the rate At which he is paid far his time
when working by the day; a considerable
portion of the year he wilt be at 'piece work,
at which he will earn considerably more money.
I cannot answer for the accuracy of these
returns, but I have never seen the amounts
disputed.

in the neighbourhood of Lincoln, the lowest

receiving 18s. At ordinary piece-work such
as tying babs for thaithing, turnip hoeing,
wheat hoeing, &c., a man can earn from 3s.
to 4s. a day; at mowing grass and seeds, ss.
to 7s. a day, and been found. On thrashing,
